The shore of the Chesapeake between Cape St. Michael—known to early settlers as the northern headland at the mouth of the Potomac—and the Patuxent is usually flat, featuring a clear, pebbly beach. This shoreline, spanning about twenty miles, is intersected by a single creek, that of St. Jerome, which flows into the bay some five or six miles north of the Potomac. The beach, occasionally interrupted by small elevations that would not be considered hills elsewhere but are notable in this area, rises just enough to offer a clear view over the expansive waters and to distinguish the inland landscape for mariners navigating up the bay. At certain points, these gentle hills end abruptly at the tide in the form of a cliff, while at others, they form a knoll that slopes down to the beach, covered in grass. This feature is visible near St. Jerome's, where the slope drops sharply to the tide line, leaving a narrow strip of low ground roughly fifty paces wide between its base and the regular water level. It was on this flat area that, in ancient times, stood the dwelling of Paul Kelpy the fisherman—a long, low building made of deal boards, constructed in the shape of a warehouse or magazine. A quarter of a mile along the beach, hidden under the brow of the slope and nearly obscured by the natural shrubbery, stood a humble cottage. Its low height allowed a man of average stature to touch the roof eaves while standing at the door. The cottage was small, with only two rooms, the largest of which was no more than ten feet square. It was constructed from hewn logs, and its door, strengthened by thick nails and a heavy padlock, offered protection against all but the most determined intruders. A small enclosure surrounded the cottage, giving room for a few common garden plants that were carefully tended. A few acres on the higher plain above the bank showed signs of cultivation, and fishing equipment scattered around, along with a skiff on the sand, indicated the livelihood of the cottage's occupant. The day before the events of our story, roughly an hour before sunset, a light drizzle fell accompanied by a steady wind from the northeast, creating a chilly gloom that enveloped the scene and heightened the feeling of solitude. A slender column of smoke curled from the cottage's chimney, indicating someone was inside, and a big, cross-eyed mastiff-bitch peeked out from beneath the eaves—guarding this lonely spot with a surly expression. The waves, pushed by the flood tide, pounded nearly against the cottage's door with a relentless, grating roar.

Relativism, a philosophical concept that suggests varying perspectives may be equally valid, has been criticized by notable philosophers such as Hilary Putnam and Susan Haack, who consider it to be misguided. John Dewey, in his book *The Quest for Certainty*, criticized what he called "the philosophical fallacy." He claimed that philosophers frequently assume categories like the mental and the physical without realizing that these are nominal concepts developed to deal with particular problems. This oversight can lead to metaphysical and conceptual confusion. Examples of this fallacy include the "ultimate Being" in Hegelian philosophy, the belief in a "realm of value," and the notion that logic, as an abstraction from concrete thought, is disconnected from the action of concrete thinking. David L. Hildebrand highlighted the problem, noting that neglecting the specific roles of inquiry has caused both realists and idealists to impose the results of deep abstraction upon experience. Pragmatists started out with the goal of transforming philosophy to better match the scientific method. They argued that idealist and realist philosophies often portrayed human knowledge as lying outside the reach of science. According to pragmatists, these philosophies often depended on either a Kant-inspired phenomenology or correspondence theories of knowledge and truth. Pragmatists criticized the former for its a priorism and the latter for its reliance on the concept of correspondence.

The concept of "human wisdom" has been a subject of debate and contemplation throughout history. In 1920, historian J. J. B. Bury suggested that the final aim of human progress for many is a society in which every individual experiences perfect happiness. However, he also acknowledged that it is impossible to prove whether humanity's unknown destination is indeed desirable. The idea of progress, Bury argued, is akin to concepts like Providence or personal immortality—it can be seen as either true or false, and its validity cannot be definitively proven or disproven. Belief in progress, therefore, is ultimately a matter of faith. In the 1980s, postmodernist thought began to challenge the grand claims made by modernizers. This movement called into question the idea of social progress itself, examining the actions and ideals of radical modernizers such as Joseph Stalin and Mao Zedong, who are frequently seen as totalitarian leaders with an exaggerated understanding of progress. Postmodernists claim that the ideas of progress from the 19th and 20th centuries, whether in capitalism or Marxism, are fundamentally flawed. They believe that these ideologies place too much emphasis on technological advancements and material wealth, neglecting the importance of inner happiness and mental peace. According to postmodernist thought, the concepts of dystopia and utopia are essentially the same, representing overarching grand narratives with unattainable conclusions. In summary, the idea of progress has been a topic of ongoing discussion and debate. Some see it as an essential and beneficial part of human growth, while others doubt its legitimacy and consequences. The postmodernist viewpoint critically analyzes conventional ideas about progress, calling for a reassessment of what genuinely defines societal advancement.

The narrative surrounding Daniel Home and his supposed supernatural abilities has been a subject of intrigue and skepticism for many years. It is said that Home possessed an extraordinary power that allowed him to transfer this energy to others, a claim that has been met with both fascination and disbelief. However, a more realistic viewpoint proposes that the events linked to Home can be accounted for by more ordinary explanations. Take, for instance, the incident involving a live coal. While some might claim that Home's ability to handle a burning coal without harm demonstrates his supernatural abilities, a more likely explanation relates to the coal's own characteristics. It's not unusual for some areas of a coal to be less active, or "dead," which makes them safe to handle. Furthermore, the description of Mr. Hall's white hair appearing "silvery" against the coal suggests that the coal was not glowing, indicating that it was likely not as hot as one might assume. The participation of Sir William Crookes, a well-known scientist, gives these events greater credibility. However, it is important to remember that even the most learned individuals can be deceived. Crookes' account of witnessing Home placing his hands in the fire lacks the precision and detail one would expect from a scientific observer. His description of Home handling a "bright red" coal is also questionable, as it doesn't consider the possibility that the coal might not have been uniformly hot. The narrative then shifts to the subject of musical phenomena, with Home once again at the center of the discussion. His alleged ability to induce spirits to play an accordion while he held it is a fascinating claim, but one that is easily explained through sleight of hand and deception. The settings in which these performances occurred—typically in low light and from behind a curtain—offered plenty of chances for trickery. The use of a cage to contain the accordion during a séance led by Sir W. Crookes presents a more challenging scenario. However, the absence of any witness to the keys moving during the performance raises questions about the authenticity of the event. The possibility of a hidden musical box or the use of hooks and loops to manipulate the accordion cannot be discounted. The tale of Mrs. Annie Eva Fay, another medium who asserted she could channel spirits through music, serves as another example of how easily deception can occur in such performances. Her séances, which involved her sitting in a circle with a bell and a guitar, were designed to create the illusion of supernatural activity. The use of darkness and Fay's presence in the circle suggests that the couple might have been collaborating to produce the look of ghostly musicians. The discovery that Mrs. Fay's performances could be recreated with basic tricks, like tape manipulation and hidden props, raises questions about the truth of her claims. The fact that she offered to reveal her secrets for a fee further undermines her credibility. In conclusion, while the stories of Daniel Home and other mediums may be captivating, it is essential to approach these accounts with a critical eye. The use of deception, sleight of hand, and the manipulation of the senses are common tools employed by those seeking to create the illusion of supernatural phenomena. As with any historical account, it is crucial to consider the context, the motivations of the individuals involved, and the possibility of alternative explanations before accepting these tales as evidence of the paranormal.

As the solemn silence was broken by the declaration "Condemned to death," a collective murmur of compassion rippled through the crowd. This was followed by a hushed silence as the rest of the document was read out. Another murmur arose upon hearing the sentences: Maroncelli to hard imprisonment for twenty years, and Pellico for fifteen. The Captain signaled for us to descend, and we cast one last glance around before returning to the court-yard. We ascended the grand staircase and were led back to the room from which we had been taken. The manacles were removed, and we were soon escorted back to San Michele. CHAPTER LIV The prisoners who had been sentenced before us had already departed for Lubiana and Spielberg, accompanied by a police commissary. He was now expected to return and guide us to our destination. However, a month passed before he arrived. To distract myself, I spent my time conversing and listening to others, including Maroncelli, who read me some of his literary works, and I reciprocated by sharing my own. One evening, I read my play "Ester d’Engaddi" from the window to Canova, Rezia, and Armari, and the following night, "Iginia d’Asti." However, at night, I became restless and miserable, struggling to sleep. I was both eager and apprehensive to learn how my family had received the news of my misfortune. Eventually, I received a letter from my father, which revealed that my last letter to him had not been sent as I had requested from the Inquisitor. This caused me great distress, as my father had been under the impression that I would be released, only to read the dreadful sentence in the Milan Gazette. I couldn't contain the contempt and anger I felt when I found out my letter had been kept from me, and I deeply understood the pain my family must have endured. Although I now believe there was no malice in this delay, I still view it as a cruel act, an eager, infernal desire to cause my loved ones immense pain. I was further enraged to learn that my companions were planning to celebrate Easter week before their departure. For me, the concept of forgiveness was beyond comprehension, and the notion of joining in such a celebration felt utterly out of reach. CHAPTER LV Finally, the German commissioner arrived and informed us that we would be departing within two days. He also shared some reassuring news: upon his return from Spielberg, he had met with the Emperor in Vienna, who had told him that our punishment would not last for twenty-four hours, but only twelve. This was meant to signify that the pain would be divided, or half the punishment remitted. Although this information was not officially communicated to us, there was no reason to doubt the commissioner's words, especially since he was open about it and it was known to the entire commission. However, I could not find solace in this news. To me, seven and a half years in chains and solitude seemed no different from fifteen; I believed it would be impossible to survive such a long period. My health had worsened, marked by intense chest pain and a constant cough, making me worry that my lungs might be damaged. I ate little and struggled to digest what I consumed. We left on the night of March 25th. We were allowed to bid farewell to our friend, Cesare Armari. A sbirro chained us in a transverse manner, linking the right hand to the left foot, making escape impossible. We boarded a gondola, with the guards rowing us towards Fusina. Upon arrival, we found two boats prepared for us. Rezia and Canova were placed in one, while Maroncelli and I were in the other. The commissary took charge of two prisoners, and an under-commissary was with the rest. Six or seven armed police guards completed our convoy, some in the boats and others in the Vetturino's box. Being forced to leave one's homeland due to misfortune is always heartbreaking, but to be uprooted in chains, exiled to a brutal climate, and imprisoned in solitary dungeons for days, hours, or even years, is a torment so unbearable that no words can fully capture its horror. Before we crossed the Alps, I realized how much my country meant to me. The sympathy we received from people of all ranks was an irresistible appeal to my affection and gratitude. In every city, village, and even the humblest of dwellings, news of our conviction had spread, and we were anticipated. In various locations, the commissioners and guards struggled to disperse the crowds that had gathered around us. It was remarkable to see the kind and compassionate sentiments shown on our behalf. In Udine, we experienced a touching incident. Upon arriving at the inn, the commissary ordered the courtyard door to be closed to keep the people at bay.

The book examines historical and mythological sources such as Eschenbach's "Parzival," the Ethiopian national epic "Kebra Nagast," the legends of Prester John, and the iconography of Chartres Cathedral. The author, Graham Hancock, posits that the Knights Templar sought the lost Ark of the Covenant and other relics at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem during the 12th century. It is suggested that an Ethiopian king in exile, possibly Lalibela, made contact with the Knights Templar while residing in Jerusalem during that time. This hypothesis is supported by the architectural legacy of Lalibela, particularly the Church of Saint George, which is intriguing in the context of Gothic architecture's development. The Ethiopian Church, concerned about the potential loss of the Ark to the Knights Templar, allegedly dispatched emissaries to Pope Clement V in 1306. The book argues that the Catholic Church's apprehension regarding the Knights Templar gaining the Ark's power was a contributing factor in Pope Clement V's decision to initiate the prosecution and arrest of the Knights Templar in 1307. The book achieved commercial success but was met with unfavorable reviews from critics. Jonathan Kirsch of the Los Angeles Times described it as a blend of travelogue, true adventure, and mystery-thriller, but primarily characterized it as amateur scholarship combined with an imaginative narrative, akin to telling ghost stories around a campfire. Desmond Ryan of the Philadelphia Inquirer humorously questioned the extent of the author's speculation.

Noir fiction, a genre characterized by its dark, moody atmosphere and morally complex characters, has a rich history that spans several decades and continents. Pioneered by American writers including Elliott Chaze, Charles Williams, Gil Brewer, Harry Whittington, Peter Rabe, and Lionel White, along with David Goodis and Jim Thompson, this literary movement has continued to develop and grow over time. In the 1980s, Black Lizard, an American publisher, played a significant role in reviving interest in noir fiction by re-releasing many classic works. Today, Akashic Books continues to celebrate the genre with a diverse collection of noir short-story anthologies. The noir genre has also found a strong foothold in Europe, with notable authors such as Jean-Claude Izzo and Massimo Carlotto contributing to its growth. According to Italian publisher Sandro Ferri, "Mediterranean noir" stands out for its exploration of the dual nature of Mediterranean life. These novels frequently portray Mediterranean cities as areas tainted by crime but still exuding an irresistible allure. The genre is defined by a dual nature, contrasting the Mediterranean way of life centered on good food, wine, friendship, and lively socializing with the darker aspects of violence, corruption, greed, and misuse of power. Among modern writers who blend the hardboiled and noir genres, James Ellroy stands out as a key figure. He describes noir as "the most scrutinized offshoot of the hard-boiled school of fiction," emphasizing its allure through the "rush of moral forfeit and the abandonment to titillation." Ellroy also recognizes the social significance of noir, pointing out its exploration of major themes like race, class, gender, and systemic problems. Noir fiction remains popular because it explores the intricacies of human nature and society, providing readers with an engaging and thought-provoking journey.

Horace Townsend, known affectionately as "H. T.," emerged from a perilous ordeal with a renewed vigor, his cheeks flushed with warmth and his body imbued with a newfound strength. He stood, barefoot and wearing only his shirt-sleeves, his hair stuck to his head and his clothes tight against his skin, an unassuming figure yet one that would earn any artist's admiration—a man who had just survived a great danger through selfless kindness. Margaret Hayley, watching his tall and upright figure, saw not the faintest trace of anything unromantic. Perhaps to her eyes, his dark complexion seemed to glow with a sort of holy light, a beacon drawing her admiration, standing in sharp contrast to the emotions she had recently felt compelled to share. It was only such deep regard that could account for her later behavior, which, for a woman of her great pride, caused a severe inner struggle that made any disaster that might have happened in the Pool's waters feel like a blessing by comparison. Halstead Rowan, confident in his admiration for his new friend's actions and not in a hurry to express it, had done what his injured hand allowed—leaping across the stream to retrieve the abandoned shoes and coat from the rock where they lay. While the rest of the group, with the exception of the distraught Mrs. Brooks Cunninghame, who was still tending to her barely revived son, gathered around the new hero to offer their thanks and congratulations, it was Margaret Hayley who took his hand. Ignoring the disapproving scowl of Captain Hector Coles, she said, "I do not know, sir, by what name to thank you—" "I believe I am right in calling you Miss Hayley," he replied, his voice still somewhat weak and tremulous. Thus, the mystery of the initials was resolved, and we can now refer to him by his full name, as those who had noticed the initials but not taken the trouble to learn his full name from the arrival book at the office had done. "I was only half-intentionally the cause of your dangerous situation, Mr. Townsend," Margaret continued, "and yet I cannot regret the liberty I took, for it may have saved a life that would have been lost, and allowed me to witness an act of selfless generosity that I will never forget, nor fail to honor for as long as I live." "You do me too much honor," he responded, his voice now a bit steadier. I have only revealed my own weakness. There was no danger to me in the water because I'm a good swimmer and can dive well. However, I must have stayed under too long, for I could not find the child immediately, and the cold water undoubtedly affected me after getting warm from climbing over the logs. That's all, and I sincerely hope we can all put this disagreeable episode behind us, as I certainly will once I manage to find some dry clothes." He spoke in a pleasant tone, though lacking the carefree enthusiasm that defined his rival of the day—the hero of the bear-stakes. As he concluded his speech, he bowed and walked away, indicating that the conversation was at an end. Margaret Hayley also stepped back and reconnected with her escort. Halstead Rowan came forward with the coat and shoes, placing them on the rock at Townsend's feet, and then took his hand with his uninjured hand, expressing a strong feeling of respect and admiration. "I'm nowhere!" he exclaimed. I challenged you across that log, but you've ventured into places I wouldn't want to follow, doing it for a noble cause, while mine was just a prank. And by the way—" They were now a little apart from the others, and Rowan spoke in a low voice, "do you know where your head lay when you came to?" "Hush! For heaven’s sake, hush! Townsend replied urgently, his look making Rowan stop talking right away. The company soon started climbing the steps, carrying the revived boy and following his mother. Townsend was able to slip the discarded shoes over his damp stockings, put on his coat, and join the rear-guard with little help. Despite the discomfort of his continued dampness, he was undoubtedly consoled by the thought that he had survived a plunge into the Pool where few men had ventured and emerged alive, and perhaps even more so by other, more complex reflections. An hour later, the entire group had returned to the Profile House, where Horace Townsend, now known by his full name, enjoyed a dry change of clothes, a slight headache, and a nap that left him refreshed as if he had bathed in the Pool for health reasons.

"Extending MARC for Subject Access," edited by Toni Petersen and Pat Molholt, is a publication by G.K. Hall that delves into the use of MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloging) for subject access in libraries. The book includes several papers on visual resources, such as "Access to Diverse Collections in University Settings: the Berkeley Dilemma" by Howard Besser and Maryly Snow, and "Visual Depictions and the Use of MARC: A View from the Trenches of Slide Librarianship" by Maryly Snow, both published in 1990. In 1991, Tim Berners-Lee began working on a hypertext graphical-user-interface (GUI) and coined the term "World Wide Web" for his program. That same year, "Facilities Standards for Art Libraries and Visual Resources Collections," edited by Betty Jo Irvine, was published by Libraries Unlimited for ARLIS/NA. Additionally, "World Architecture Index: a Guide to Illustrations," compiled by Edward H. Teague, was released by Greenwood Press as part of its Art Reference Collection No. 12. The Visual Resources Association (VRA) established its listserv, VRA-L, in 1992, providing a crucial communication tool for its members who are visual resources curators. In 1993, Oxford University Press published the "Users' Guide to The Art and Architecture Thesaurus" alongside the electronic edition. The VRA formed its Data Standards Committee in March 1994. In September of that same year, Marc Andreessen left the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) to found Mosaic Communications Corp, which would eventually evolve into Netscape. Mosaic's launch marked the beginning of the World Wide Web for the general public. In 1994, the first image database, SPIRO, was launched on the World Wide Web. In 1995, the "Concordance of Ancient Site Names" was edited and published, adding to the expanding collection of work on visual resources and subject access in libraries.

The fascinating tale of carrier pigeons, a breed naturally gifted with the ability to return home from vast distances, has captivated people for centuries. These birds have been tested by being carried hundreds of miles across the sea, yet they always find their way back with perfect precision. This remarkable ability has been highly valuable in many human activities, especially in wars, where they have been employed to carry messages through enemy territory. A notable example was when the German Emperor, intrigued by their reliability, sent a group of these pigeons from England to Germany. Released from Dover, they all made their way back to Düsseldorf within six hours, an occurrence that caused both fascination and worry among the English, prompting a debate in the House of Commons. In another intriguing find, a rock in the Magdalena district of Sonora, Mexico, was discovered to be inscribed with characters remarkably similar to Chinese script. A knowledgeable Chinese person verified the inscription as genuine, stating it is over two thousand years old and indicates the presence of a Chinese community in the area. This challenges the commonly held belief that Columbus was the first to discover the Americas, suggesting that Chinese explorers may have reached the continent much earlier. Evidence of large-scale Chinese sea expeditions during the early periods of civilization has also been discovered in the Pacific Islands and Australia. King Menelik of Abyssinia appointed a Russian General as Governor-General over the equatorial provinces, showing his intent to introduce civilization to his people. M. M. de Leontieff, who had earlier traveled to Abyssinia and carried gifts from the Czar, is anticipated to make a positive contribution to the country's progress, similar to how General Gordon contributed in Egypt. The text highlights the unity of humanity, indicating that the differences between nations are small, much like the varied abilities present in one family. It shows how environmental factors, like climate and lifestyle, can greatly affect a population's physical traits over time, as observed in the descendants of people with lighter skin who live in tropical areas. The author suggests that human races have developed separately from the original human family, each acquiring distinct features due to local conditions over thousands of years. The search for the history and origins of different countries is compared to finding distant relatives, stirring interest in their paths and the causes of their separation from their ancestors. The author recognizes the limits of written records, which date back only a few centuries, and emphasizes the value of alternative historical sources like inscriptions on monuments and walls. However, the narrative also recognizes the immense span of time prior to the existence of writing, leaving the stories of early humans to be reconstructed from fragments and interpretations.

Postmodernism is a complex and multifaceted cultural and intellectual movement that emerged in the mid-20th century. It is defined by doubt, relativism, and a widespread skepticism toward major theories and ideological systems. Postmodernism has made a major influence across many areas such as music, art, literature, and philosophy. In the realm of music, postmodernism has manifested in diverse and innovative ways. Jonathan Kramer, an expert in the field, has noted that avant-garde works, which some might classify as modernist, frequently question and expand the conventional limits of what is regarded as music. These compositions can be provocative and unsettling, pushing the listener to reconsider their understanding of the art form. In the 1960s, a group of composers such as Terry Riley, Henryk Górecki, Bradley Joseph, John Adams, Steve Reich, Philip Glass, Michael Nyman, and Lou Harrison aimed to distance themselves from the perceived elitism and dissonance of atonal academic modernism. They created music with simpler textures and more consonant harmonies, offering a fresh perspective on musical expression. Concurrently, artists like John Cage questioned the established notions of beauty and objectivity that were prevalent in modernism. Cage's work often incorporated unconventional sounds and methods, further expanding the definition of music. Alongside these advancements in classical and avant-garde music, postmodernism has also shaped various popular music genres. Dominic Strinati, an author on postmodernism, highlights the significance of "art rock" and the blending of styles seen in the works of groups like Talking Heads and performers such as Laurie Anderson. The Pet Shop Boys' self-conscious reinvention of disco is another example of postmodern musical innovation. In the late 20th century, American singer Madonna was dubbed by avant-garde academics as the "personification of the postmodern." Both Christian writer Graham Cray and literary critic Olivier Sécardin argued that Madonna embodies postmodernism, while Martin Amis referred to her as "perhaps the most postmodern figure on the planet." Her constantly evolving image and style, along with her talent for reinventing herself, have made her a symbol of the postmodern era. In philosophy, postmodernism arose in the 1970s as a wide range of thinkers started to challenge and examine the prevailing narratives and ideologies of their era. These philosophers often rejected the idea of objective truth and universal values, instead advocating for a more nuanced and context-dependent understanding of knowledge and reality. Overall, postmodernism has had a profound impact on various aspects of culture and society, challenging traditional norms and encouraging a more open and questioning approach to art, music, and thought.

Hildebrand Gurlitt was a well-known German art dealer in the Nazi period. From 1939 to 1944, he obtained many artworks, aside from those he kept for his own collection. From these acquisitions, 168 pieces were intended for the Führermuseum, a museum envisioned by Adolf Hitler to showcase his ideal of German art. Gurlitt took advantage of his officially sanctioned trips to Paris, a city filled with artworks of uncertain origins, some of which are now known to have been stolen. These trips enabled him to grow his collection of artwork and accumulate significant wealth through commissions, as the Nazi regime paid large amounts for art purchases. Besides his official responsibilities, Gurlitt also bought paintings personally, especially from artists targeted by the Nazis. One example was Max Beckmann, who had been in exile in the Netherlands by 1944. In September 1944, Gurlitt and his associate, Erhard Göpel, the local buyer for Hitler's Führermuseum, purchased five works from Beckmann. One of the paintings acquired was "Bar, Brown," which Gurlitt kept for himself. After Gurlitt passed away, his wife put the painting up for sale, but it didn't sell. Some time later, his son Cornelius sold it at a Ketterer auction in Stuttgart in 1972, where it sold for DM 90,000 after deducting the auctioneer's fees. The same painting was subsequently put up for sale at Sotheby's in London and sold for £1.2 million. Beckmann's family did not challenge the distribution of the sale proceeds, viewing Gurlitt's initial purchase as legitimate, even though it occurred during difficult times for the artist. After the war, Gurlitt was captured along with his wife.

Conrad Martens, an artist active from 1835 until his death in 1878, was best known for his landscape paintings. His work is recognized for its capacity to blend the landscape in a way that appeals to European tastes. Martens' watercolour studies of Sydney Harbour are highly regarded, as they introduced Romantic ideals into his paintings. He is also remembered for joining Charles Darwin on the HMS Beagle, a voyage that Augustus Earle also participated in. Between 1851 and 1885, the Victorian gold rush led to a significant influx of settlers and an increase in wealth. The artist S. T. Gill (1818–1880) recorded life on the Australian goldfields, capturing the spirit of the time. However, the colonial art market at that time was more focused on landscape paintings. These were often commissioned by wealthy landowners or merchants who wanted to showcase their prosperity. One notable landscape painting from this period is "Flood in the Darling" by William Piguenit, created between 1836 and 1914, which was purchased by the National Gallery of New South Wales in 1895. Other well-known artists of that era were Eugene von Guerard, Nicholas Chevalier, William Strutt, John Skinner Prout, and Knud Bull. Louis Buvelot played an important role in landscape painting during the later period. Influenced by the Barbizon school, Buvelot embraced a plein air method, painting outdoors to capture the natural light and atmosphere. His work frequently depicted a more tranquil and settled portrayal of the land, differing from the earlier focus on unfamiliarity or peril in Australian landscape art. Buvelot's method, along with his significant impact as a teacher, has earned him the title of "Father of Australian landscape painting" from some.

Otto Grashof was a German painter, illustrator, and portraitist recognized for his unique artistic contributions. Thomas Somerscales was an English seascape painter, renowned for his work such as "The Naval Battle of Iquique." In addition to these notable figures, there were several lesser-known painters of the same period whose works, though not widely celebrated, are significant. These are John Searle, María Graham, Johan Heinrich Jenny, Francis Martín Drexel, Camilo Domeniconi, Augusto Borget, Procesa del Carmen Sarmiento, Juan Bianchi, Clara Filleul, Alexander Simón, Giovatto Molinelli, and Theodor Ohlsen. The Chilean Precursors of Chilean painting were a group of artists who, similar to their foreign contemporaries working in Chile, were influenced by European art. These Chilean painters didn't stick to one style but were active at the same time and played a key role in starting a new era of Chilean art through the founding of the Chilean Academy of Painting. Galaz and Ivaelic observed that these artists' works were deeply tied to the Chilean landscape, its people, and cultural aspects. Among the Chilean painters in this movement, Manuel Antonio Caro is the most outstanding artist of that period. His style was realistic, frequently portraying customs and folkloric scenes. Some of his most renowned works are "La Zamacueca" and "The Abdication of O’Higgins," and Caro also joined the newly established academy. Francisco Javier Mandiola was another key figure in this movement, recognized for depicting local customs and regarded as the most gifted student of Raymond. His work helped enrich the artistic landscape of Chile during this time, highlighting the country's varied cultural and social elements.

In his essay on gardening, Horace Walpole discusses a concept that exemplifies a fundamental principle: the modern style of gardening originated from Bridgeman's invention of the "ha-ha," a pioneering approach in landscape gardening. The "ha-ha" allowed a garden to blend harmoniously with the surrounding countryside, separated only by an invisible barrier rather than a wall. This idea questions the belief that a garden enthusiast would favor nature over art, since a garden itself is an artistic endeavor that substitutes the raw wilderness. The love for nature, as seen in later figures like Lord Byron, can sometimes border on misanthropy, praising the wild for its own sake. However, the landscape gardener believes that their art should be subordinate to nature, incorporating the wider scenery into their designs rather than excluding it. This perspective echoes the views of Telford, who considered rivers as existing to supply canals, and Gilpin, who evaluated nature through the lens of the "theory of the picturesque." Gilpin observed that although nature's compositions might appear cold and singular, they never fall into "mannerism." In other words, nature is a sublime landscape artist whose work must be embraced and integrated by the human gardener. An interesting example of this theory appears in a lecture by Henry Tilney from Jane Austen's "Mansfield Park," where Walpole's idea suggests that the creation of the "ha-ha" reflects an increasing partnership between humans and nature, as well as between landowners and the countryside. This alliance is characterized by improved roads and inns, the gradual integration of urban and rural areas, and a growing awareness of the drawbacks of overpopulated cities. The love for nature has deep roots, as poets from Chaucer onward have celebrated the beauty of landscapes, the coming of spring, and the grandeur of storms and sunsets. The Pope school's indifference toward nature was a fleeting occurrence, showcasing the confidence of the urban populace and their contempt for the rural realm. However, the squire class maintained a strong affection for field sports, and as they became influenced by urban ideas, they began expressing emotions that were clearly reflected in works such as Izaak Walton's "The Compleat Angler." The older poets frequently used nature as a setting for human activities, emphasizing specific details and the pleasures of outdoor games or country pastimes. They adhered to old conventions and engaged in conversations with imaginary shepherds, Robin Hood, or allegorical knights in romantic forests. In contrast, during Pope's time, nature emerged as an abstract or metaphysical deity that could be worshipped with a distinct appreciation. Pope himself, influenced by Bolingbroke and Shaftesbury, expounded on the stars and the animal world in his "Essay on Man." Shaftesbury, in particular, emphasized the aesthetic perspective of nature, asserting that the Good, the True, and the Beautiful are all one, and that the universe impresses us as an artistic embodiment of harmony. This viewpoint spurred a genuine appreciation for beauty, evident in works such as Akenside's "The Pleasures of Imagination" and Henry Brooke's "Universal Beauty." James Thomson's "The Seasons," particularly its elegant "Hymn of Nature," exemplifies this sentimental trend. Thomson's descriptions of nature, intended to serve as a sermon, show a growing interest in country life and a challenge to the supremacy of the urban wit. However, Thomson's philosophy and observation remain somewhat separate, and his masterpiece, the didactic poem on "Liberty," remains largely forgotten. In conclusion, the love for nature has changed over time, shifting from serving as a background for human activities to being cherished and revered as something valuable in itself. The landscape gardener's approach to subordinating art to nature and incorporating the wider scenery into their designs reflects a growing appreciation for the beauty and harmony of the natural world.

He was a jay, indeed, and I had just witnessed his rather cad-like behavior towards Mrs. Bevidge," one character remarked. "Then I'm at a loss as to why you were in his company," another responded. "Oh, you do understand, Alan. You mustn't apply logic here! It's like questioning how you became more serious than sober." The brother laughed, unable to argue. "It was the excitement," he explained. "But you can't indulge in such behavior, Bess," he chided, his tone heavy with the weight of his own past mistakes. "I know I shouldn't, but I do," she retorted. "I understand it's detrimental to me, if not to others. Let's make a pact to stop!" "I'm always ready to make such a promise," the young man agreed, his voice tinged with melancholy. He added, "But you have a sharp mind, Bess, and I dislike seeing you act foolishly." "Do you truly, Alan?" the girl inquired, seemingly pleased by his criticism as much as his compliment. "Do you think I have a sharp mind?" "You're the only girl who does," he affirmed. "Oh, I didn't mean to ask for that much! But why can't I utilize it effectively? Other girls draw, play music, write. I only seek the excitement that's bad for me. I wish you could explain it." Alan Lynde did not attempt to answer. The question seemed to redirect his thoughts inward, causing him to feel disheartened. "I possess a sharp mind too, I believe," he began. "Loads of them!" his sister interjected, generously. "There's no man who can compare to you. If I could talk to you constantly, I wouldn't need the company of jays. I'm not flattering you. You're always a feast of reason; I have no interest in emotional outpourings. You always take the right view of things when you're being yourself, and even when you're not, you're not stupid. You could be anything you chose." "The problem is that I can't choose," he replied. "Yes, I suppose that is the problem," she agreed. "You shouldn't use such language, Bess," her brother admonished, sternly. "Oh, I don't with everyone," she defended herself. "Never with ladies!" He glanced at her with a smile that was both rueful and humorous. "You got me, I guess," he admitted. "'Touché,' Mr. Durgin says. He fences and speaks French. It's like an animal trying to speak French; you always expect them to speak English. But I don't mind your swearing in my presence; I know it helps to dissipate the tension." She laughed, and coaxed a laugh from him as well. "Is there anything to him?" he asked, once their laughter subsided. "Yes, quite a bit," Bessie replied thoughtfully, and then she went on to recount all that Jeff had told her about himself, describing his composure in dealing with the benevolent Mrs. Bevidge, as she referred to her, and sketching his character as she perceived it. Her sketch was filled with astute conjectures and she made it entertaining for her brother, who, from his own perspective of mischief, undoubtedly judged the original more intelligently. "Well, you'd better avoid him after this," he advised at the end. "Yes," she agreed pensively. "I suppose it's like developing a taste for a very common type of whiskey, isn't it? I see what you mean. If one must indulge, it should be in champagne." She turned to him with a look of keen yet limited understanding, which always makes women's conjectures about vice so amusing or so touching to men. "Better avoid the champagne as well," her brother suggested darkly. "Yes, I know," she said, sinking back into her chair and staring dreamily into the fire. After a while, she asked abruptly, "Will you stop if I will?" "I'm afraid I couldn't," he replied. "You could try," she encouraged. "Oh, I'm used to it," he said. "Then it's a deal," she declared, leaping from her chair and striding over to him. She ran her fingers through his hair, smoothing it over his forehead, then pressed a kiss to the spot she had just touched, even though it was damp and unpleasant against her lips. "Poor boy, poor boy! Now, remember! No more jays for me, and no more sprees for you. Jeff Durgin wasn't sure if Miss Bessie Lynde planned to attend Mrs. Bevidge's Thursday gatherings or not.

Graphic Identity: In 2016, the Chicago-based graphic design firm Thirst was commissioned to develop the graphic identity for the Exhibit Columbus. Their work played a crucial role in establishing a cohesive and recognizable visual representation for the project, enhancing its overall impact and appeal.

The idea of holding no opinion, referred to as [Greek: epochê], is a condition that results in a feeling of peace known as [Greek: ataraxia]. Pyrrho, a philosopher whose questions were posed in a manner reminiscent of Kant, sought not to develop a system of truth but to explore the nature of philosophy itself. His dedication to this pursuit is illustrated by an anecdote from Diogenes, in which Pyrrho was found talking to himself, contemplating how to become a virtuous person ([Greek: chrêstos]). This story reveals a depth of character distinct from the typical skepticism found in Sextus' works. The essence of Pyrrho's philosophy and his approach to life can be largely attributed to his personal disposition. His indifference was inherent to his calm nature and was not solely a product of his philosophical beliefs. While this attitude could be aspired to, it could never be fully replicated. One of his followers noted that to truly embrace Pyrrho's teachings, one must possess a similar temperament. Diogenes records that Pyrrho was the first to propose the rudimentary principles of skepticism, although his ideas were not yet fully developed, as he left no written works. There is no evidence of Pyrrho formulating the Tropes, but it is likely that he recognized some contradictions in sensory experiences, possibly hinting at the Tropes in a nascent form. Among the many skeptical maxims, or [Greek: phônai], the three that are most closely associated with the origins of skepticism are the [Greek: antilogia], the [Greek: ouden horizô], and the [Greek: ou mallon]. Diogenes cites Protagoras as the source for the idea that there are always two opposing arguments for everything. The phrase "to determine nothing" is attributed to Timon's _Python_, and the other two maxims are also linked to him by Aristocles. The Greek expression [Greek: ou mallon] is directly associated with Democritus, though Pyrrho's interpretation of it may have differed, as noted by Sextus. It is probable that Pyrrho employed all three of these sayings, as suggested by Diogenes. However, this led to accusations from the Dogmatics that the Skeptics were dogmatizing simply by possessing such sayings. Sextus countered this by claiming that these maxims also carry their own meaning, much like a purgative eliminates itself along with other harmful elements. In comparing the later Pyrrhonism with the teachings of Pyrrho, there is a stark contrast in the moral stance of the two. For Pyrrho, the equilibrium of the soul was a means to apply to his positive theory of life, whereas for the later Pyrrhoneans, it was the ultimate goal. However, the empirical tendency that characterized the history of Pyrrhonism can be traced back to Pyrrho as its originator. He was an empirical philosopher, and his influence in this regard was in stark contrast to the dialectical spirit of Academic Skepticism. The empiricism of the school is evident in its scientific knowledge, the fact that many Skeptics were physicians, and in the nature of the ten Tropes of [Greek: epochê]. It is safe to assert that the foundational principles of Pyrrhonism are attributable to Pyrrho and his originality, which gave the school its strength. However, the more elaborate arguments and the specifics of its maxims belong to later periods. Regarding the relationship between Pyrrhonism and the Academy, the connection is challenging to pinpoint with precision, especially between the time of Pyrrho and Aenesidemus. However, skepticism within the Academy was never entirely the same as Pyrrhonism, even though there were periods in the history of the Academy when the difference was minimal. Arcesilaus, who brought doubt into the Academy, sought to revive the dialectic method of Socrates. He replaced lectures with discussions, which he believed to be a more Socratic method of teaching. Despite Sextus' assertion that Arcesilaus' skepticism was the closest to Pyrrhonism, his teachings were fundamentally rooted in the dialectical principle, which was in opposition to the empiricism of Pyrrho. The belief in the existence of absolute truth, as held by Socrates and Plato, never completely lost its influence over the Academy. This belief eventually led the Academy back to Dogmatism and paved the way for the Eclecticism that marked its departure from history. The histories of Pyrrhonism and Academic Skepticism were contemporaneous for some time. Timon, the immediate follower of Pyrrho and referred to by Sextus as the "prophet of Pyrrho," was a contemporary of Arcesilaus. His decision not to join the Academy and his writings suggest that he saw the Academy's skepticism as distinct from Pyrrhonism.

Hans Melzian, a scholar, has contributed significantly to the understanding of the Bini language, which is predominantly spoken in Southern Nigeria. His work, "A Concise Dictionary of the Bini Language," is a valuable resource for those interested in this linguistic field. The dictionary can be freely downloaded, borrowed, and streamed via the Internet Archive. In addition to Melzian's work, another important document related to the region is the autobiography of Jacob Egharevba, titled "ITAN ẸDAGBỌN MWEN." This autobiography is written in the Edo language, which is another significant language in Nigeria. The Edo language is spoken by the Edo people, who primarily reside in the Edo State of Nigeria. These works offer valuable insights into the languages and cultures of Southern Nigeria, helping readers gain a better understanding of the region's linguistic diversity. Having these resources available online enables a broader audience to access and appreciate Nigeria's rich linguistic heritage.

The article examines the controversy over Seth Rich's death, a DNC staffer, and the media's response to it. Rod Wheeler, a private investigator, was hired by Rodger Stone and a wealthy Trump supporter, Ed Butowsky, to investigate Rich's murder. There were claims that Rich had leaked DNC emails to WikiLeaks, but these allegations have been largely debunked. In May 2017, Fox News published a story suggesting a link between Rich and the FBI, which was later retracted. The story relied on Wheeler's investigation, but he later stated that the quotes attributed to him were made up. Wheeler sued Fox News for defamation, alleging that the network had manipulated his claims. The lawsuit was dismissed in August 2018, with the judge ruling that there was no evidence of manipulation. Butowsky also faced a lawsuit from the Rich family, who accused him of exploiting their son's death for political purposes. The lawsuit was dismissed for the same reasons as Wheeler's, as the judge found no proof that Butowsky had done anything wrong. It’s worth noting that the allegations linking Rich, the DNC, and WikiLeaks have been thoroughly debunked by numerous investigations, including those carried out by the U.S. intelligence community. The consensus among experts is that Russia was responsible for the hacking of the DNC's computer systems and the subsequent release of emails. In conclusion, the Seth Rich story has been a source of much controversy and misinformation. While some individuals have sought to use the incident to advance their political agendas, the evidence overwhelmingly points to Russia as the culprit behind the DNC hacking. It is crucial for the public to critically evaluate the information presented in the media and to rely on credible sources for accurate news.

Suppose a President were elected on the promise of expanding military forces immediately following a European war. To consider the potential consequences further would be an insult to our intelligence. The creation of "defensive" alliances, whether directed against or in support of us—assuming we could convince others to participate—would result in rising tensions, provocations, and a replay of previous historical conflicts. However, if such a devastating war were to happen, it wouldn't be a tragedy if we had brought it upon ourselves. The real tragedy would be if we failed to recognize the inherent worth that Germany holds, which makes our actions justified. The true sorrow would be that we were so preoccupied with the faults of others that we neglected to address our own shortcomings. I am woman: as ancient as the Lebanon cedars and older still; as young as the fresh green shoot pushing through the snow in March. My face is turned to the East, flushed with the dawn of my potential; my hands are restrained by the binding touch of the solitary woman who, driven by desire, knew only the need for a kiss on her throat and a child in the curve of her arm. Today, I am a woman—somewhat less, yet a little more—because I am learning to sing not his song, nor another's, but my own, which has lived in my heart since the first day. It will be a grand golden song, though not always gentle with a sweet cadence, for I must work to sing it. I am learning to live on nothing and still feel full, to keep my cold limbs warm without fire, and to keep going on my journey without a kiss or a child, even though my lips are red and my arms are ready. Yet I know I will never stop until I've sung every single note. Even in the distant days ahead, as they call to me in the rosy dawn, I will remain a woman. My song will become sweetly familiar, and he who was once frightened will draw near, singing his separate song, always his own, yet blending its masculine tones with mine. Together, we will create a grand harmony that envelops the world in our music, rejoicing once more in our union. That day will come... But today, I'm tired—the East is painted pink with the hope of dawn. (The following is one of the poems in Edgar Lee Master’s “Spoon River Anthology” which has been featured in Reedy’s St. Louis Mirror and has garnered widespread attention. In our opinion, it is among the finest poetry.) Caroline Branson With our hearts like drifting suns, had we only walked as often before the April fields until starlight softened the darkness under the rock, our trysting place in the wood, where the brook turns! Had we only moved from courtship like musical notes blending, into the inspired spontaneity of love! But to forsake the magic of the body, where our souls would swoon, plunging into a world where time, space, and our separate identities dissolved—obliterated by love! To give up these experiences for a room with lamps; to stand with our secret laughing at itself, concealed among flowers and mandolins, watched by all between salad and coffee. To witness his trembling and feel my own premonition, as if signing a bond—not ablaze with gifts and pledges heaped with rosy hands over his brow. And then, O night! Deliberate! Unlovely! With all our courtship wiped away by the act of love in a chosen room at an hour known to all. The next day, he sat listless, almost cold, changed in a strange way, puzzling over why I was crying, until a sense of sick despair mixed with a wild longing took hold of us, driving us to make the pact of death. A slender strand of the Earth's sphere, delicate as starlight, waits to be pulled once more into the current of creation. But next time, I will be born under the watchful eyes of Raphael and St. Francis as they walk by. For I am their little brother, to be clearly known face to face in a cycle of birth that lies ahead. You may know the seed and the soil; you may feel the cold rain fall. But only the earth and sky know the secret of the seed in the nuptial chamber beneath the soil. Throw me into the stream again, give me another trial—Save me, Shelley!
