The Phoenician civilization, known for its maritime prowess and trade networks, has long been a subject of fascination and speculation regarding its influence on other cultures. One such debate revolves around the possibility of Phoenician contact with ancient American civilizations. However, the evidence for this theory is limited and frequently contested. The Phoenicians are credited with developing an early form of the alphabet, which has influenced the writing systems used across Europe and Southwestern Asia today. This script is different from the writing systems of ancient American civilizations, like those at Palenque and Copan. The inscriptions in these American sites bear no resemblance to Phoenician writing, nor do they share any characteristics with the Phoenician language or architectural styles. In 1872, a stone purportedly inscribed with Phoenician script was discovered in Paraíba, Brazil. The inscription allegedly told the story of a Phoenician ship that was separated from a fleet sailing from Egypt around Africa during a storm. It also mentioned a pharaoh, either Necho I or Necho II. The stone was initially accepted as genuine by Ladislau de Souza Mello Netto, the director of the National Museum of Brazil. However, by 1873, the philologist Ernest Renan had persuaded Netto that the inscription was a forgery, since the letter forms did not match those used by the Phoenicians. The absence of a shared linguistic or written tradition between the Phoenicians and ancient American societies, combined with doubts about the Paraíba stone's authenticity, complicates efforts to confirm a real link between these two cultures. Although the notion of Phoenician influence on American civilizations is fascinating, the existing evidence does not back this theory. Further research and discovery may shed more light on this topic in the future, but for now, the relationship between the Phoenicians and ancient American cultures remains speculative.

Christianity holds that one can determine God's existence, whereas atheism denies this, stating that God does not exist. Agnosticism, on the other hand, maintains a neutral stance, arguing that there is insufficient evidence to definitively confirm or deny the existence of a higher power. In an essay, the philosopher Bertrand Russell suggests that extraordinary personal experiences, such as hearing a voice from the sky predicting specific events that later transpire, could potentially sway one's belief towards the existence of a superhuman intelligence. Leslie Weatherhead, a Christian theologian (1893–1976), presented a more refined view of agnosticism in his 1965 work, "The Christian Agnostic," arguing that many people who identify as agnostics might have a deeper grasp of God than some frequent attendees of church who hold incorrect beliefs about the divine. Although Weatherhead's ideas were seen as radical and off-putting by traditional theologians, his version of agnosticism is actually less extreme than Thomas Huxley's, who is commonly called "Darwin's Bulldog." Weatherhead held that the human soul has an innate ability to either reject or accept God, based on the fundamental nature of free will, yet he was certain that, in the end, no one would choose to turn away from the divine. In the United States, Robert G. Ingersoll (1833–1899), an Illinois lawyer, politician, and famous 19th-century orator, became known as "The Great Agnostic." His skepticism and critical analysis of religious dogma, especially in an 1896 speech, helped establish him as a leading figure in the agnostic movement.

Mersenne, a well-known philosopher and scientist from the 17th century, held the view that scientific investigation could establish laws and rules governing sense-perceptions. He opposed the notion of doubting everything by pointing out several arguments: 1. People generally agree on certain facts, like the fact that an ant is smaller than an elephant. 2. Natural laws, like optics, guide our sense perceptions and help correct inaccuracies. 3. Human-made tools such as rulers and scales are used to measure and dispel uncertainty regarding phenomena like bent oars, pigeons' necks, and round towers. However, a Pyrrhonist could respond by pointing out that the senses can be misleading, resulting in an infinite regression or circular reasoning. Mersenne countered this by arguing that widely accepted rules can be proposed and examined over time to confirm their reliability. He also noted that if everything is subject to doubt, then doubt itself can be questioned, suggesting that some degree of certainty is essential. Mersenne thought that mathematical, physical, and other scientific knowledge, which has been thoroughly tested, is valid and has real-world applications. He was among the few philosophers who embraced Thomas Hobbes' radical ideas, viewing them as a new science of human behavior. Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679) was deeply engaged with prominent skeptics such as Gassendi and Mersenne throughout his extended time in Paris. Although Hobbes shared an interest in skepticism and epistemology with his peers, he developed a distinct viewpoint that set him apart from them.

Renaissance Humanism was a major intellectual movement that arose during the Renaissance in Europe. It was characterized by a renewed interest in the study of classical antiquity, particularly the literature, philosophy, and art of ancient Greece and Rome. This movement aimed to restore the values and knowledge from the ancient world and integrate them into modern society. One of the leading figures in the development of Renaissance Humanism was Lovato Lovato, an Italian poet and scholar. He was followed by other prominent humanists such as Leonardo Bruni, who further advanced the movement. The origins and evolution of humanism during this period have been extensively studied and documented by scholars like Ronald Witt in his work "In the Footsteps of the Ancients: The Origins of Humanism from Lovato to Bruni," published by Brill Publishers in 2000. Another important aspect of Renaissance Humanism was the influence of paganism. Edgar Wind's book *Pagan Mysteries in the Renaissance*, published by W.W. Norton in 1969, examines how pagan beliefs and practices influenced the cultural and intellectual environment of the Renaissance. This book provides valuable insights into the complex relationship between Christianity and paganism during this period. Charles, in "The Scope of Renaissance Humanism," published by the University of Michigan Press in 1983, offers a comprehensive analysis of the movement, its impact on various aspects of society, and the key figures who contributed to its development. For those interested in learning more about Renaissance Humanism, there are several external resources available. The World History Encyclopedia offers a general overview of Renaissance Humanism, and Albert Rabil Jr.'s "Humanism 1: An Outline" serves as a brief introduction to the subject. Additionally, the Library of Congress's article titled "Rome Reborn: The Vatican Library & Renaissance Culture: Humanism," published on July 1, 2002, examines the Vatican Library's role in preserving and spreading humanist ideas. Furthermore, the BBC Radio 4 program "In Our Time" included a conversation about "Paganism in the Renaissance" featuring Tom Healy, Charles Hope, and Evelyn Welch on June 16, 2005. This discussion provides an engaging and informative perspective on the influence of paganism during the Renaissance period. In short, Renaissance Humanism was a key intellectual movement that aimed to revive and apply the knowledge and values of classical antiquity to the modern world. The study of this movement offers a deeper understanding of the cultural and intellectual transformations that took place during the Renaissance.

The Ministry of Love in George Orwell's dystopian novel "Nineteen Eighty-Four" plays a vital role. It is tasked with "rehabilitating" thought criminals, who are subsequently released as loyal subjects, completely brainwashed to worship Big Brother, thereby fulfilling the name of the Ministry. In different film versions of the novel, the character of Big Brother has been depicted in varying ways. In the 1954 BBC adaptation, production designer Roy Oxley was shown in a single still photograph. The 1956 film adaptation depicted Big Brother as a stern-looking disembodied head illustration. In the 1984 film starring John Hurt, the photograph of Big Brother was that of actor Bob Flag. Both Oxley and Flag had small mustaches. Since "Nineteen Eighty-Four" was published, the term "Big Brother" has come to be commonly used as a metaphor for any intrusive or overly controlling authority figure, as well as for government surveillance efforts. The idea of Big Brother and other Orwellian symbols are frequently used in the joke called the Russian reversal. In their 1956 book *Blood Royal*, Iain Moncreiffe and Don Pottinger jokingly included the line: "Without Little Father, no need for Big Brother," referencing the Russian Revolution and the Soviet Union. The global reality TV series "Big Brother" draws inspiration from the novel's idea of ongoing surveillance. In 2000, following the debut of the U.S. version of the CBS show "Big Brother," the Estate of George Orwell sued CBS and its production company, Orwell Productions, Inc., in a federal court in Chicago.

The phrase "Living by the Sword" has been used in different contexts to express the notion that those who depend on violence or aggression will eventually face the consequences of their actions. This idea originates from historical and religious writings, indicating that the use of force often leads to a continued cycle of violence. In popular culture, the phrase has been referenced in music. For instance, in Megadeth's song "Five Magics," frontman Dave Mustaine includes the line "He who lives by the sword, will surely also die," which echoes the sentiment of the proverb. Similarly, Bob Seger's song "Night Moves" features the phrase "Living by the Sword" in its third verse, further highlighting the phrase's cultural influence. The idea of living by the sword is frequently contrasted with Christian pacifism, which advocates for nonviolence and resolving conflicts peacefully. The phrase "beat swords into ploughshares" is also related, as it suggests the transformation of weapons into tools for peaceful purposes, symbolizing the shift from a violent to a peaceful society. While the phrase "living by the sword" has been used to discuss the consequences of a violent lifestyle, it is important to note that the interpretation and application of this concept can vary depending on the context in which it is used. As such, readers are encouraged to explore various perspectives and sources to form their own understanding of the phrase and its implications.

In the Scholastic philosophical tradition, the idea of the soul plays a key role in explaining the nature of living creatures. Thomas Aquinas and other Thomists argue that members of the same genus share an essence, varying only in their accidents and substantial form. The soul is considered the substantial form that distinguishes living beings from each other. Plants have what is called a "vegetative soul," which is responsible for their growth and development. Animals, on the other hand, are endowed with "sensitive souls," granting them the ability to perceive and react to their environment. Human beings are unique in having "intellectual souls," which are marked by reason and immortality. Aristotle's perspective on the soul is one of unity, with the soul being a single entity endowed with five distinct groups of faculties, or "dunámeis." These faculties are: 1. The "vegetative" faculty (threptikón), which is concerned with the maintenance and development of organic life. 2. The appetite (oretikón) signifies the inclination to pursue what is perceived as good. 3. The faculty of sense perception, known as aisthetikón, allows for the perception of the external world. 4. The "locomotive" faculty (kinetikón), which governs bodily movements. 5. Reason (dianoetikón), the most elevated faculty, is linked to intellectual and rational thought. Scholastic philosophers typically adhere to Aristotle's classification, considering the body and soul as a single integrated entity. The soul is regarded as the "forma substantialis," or the vital principle, which is the origin of all activities. Therefore, the study of the soul includes functions that are now commonly linked to biology and physiology. The connection between the mind and the body falls under philosophical or metaphysical discussion. When considering human appetite, it can be split into two aspects: the rational and the irrational. The rational part is called the will, and the irrational part is called passion. In the field of ethics, Thomas Aquinas aligns with Aristotle's view that happiness is "an operation according to perfect virtue," and he also claims that happiness is a distinctly human condition, attained through the practice of virtue. This perspective emphasizes the importance of moral and intellectual development in achieving a fulfilling and meaningful life.

"Very well, then," came the response, "but in exchange for my silence, you must inquire whether Kate has sewn the tassel on my smoking-cap as she promised." "Of course I did," a cheerful voice replied. Kate stepped out of the parlor holding the cap, looking more beautiful than ever. "Ah, thank you, dear Kate! Make sure to keep Paul in good spirits while I go enjoy my cigar. It would be rude to leave him alone." Kate smiled, and their planned walk on the piazza was replaced with a stroll down the avenue. It must have been a lovely walk, because when the tea bell rang, they were still there, watching the pale moon rise and wondering to themselves how often they would share such moments with the same joy. They didn't wonder for long. Each night, Paul Linden would invite someone for a walk, and somehow, everyone was exhausted except Kate, and everyone was occupied except Kate. It wasn't long before the whispering leaves bore witness to a pledge of love between the two, and heard (if leaves could hear) what Paul Linden considered the softest music on earth—the low tones that conveyed to him the surrender of sweet Kate de la Croix's heart. The leaves saw a strange ring gleaming on her fair hand, and they remained discreet—but not the sisters. Minnie noticed the tiny sign of their shared faith, and sorrowful Kate told her secret to her in tears and sobs. Even though she was unhappy that night, remembering the burst of grief that came after the secret was revealed, another bird had already left the nest by the time the wedding was over. Mr. de la Croix smoked an unusually large number of cigars that evening when his daughter departed, and the sisters tried to remain cheerful; but none of them went to bed without entering Kate's empty room to weep anew. Lisa had to threaten to turn it into a storage room for rags before they could get used to passing by without entering and mourning her absence as if she would never return. "Don't keep crying over Kate," she would say, "she'll be back, and you should wait until then to be happy." "But we miss her so much, Lisa," said Rose, her eyes full of tears. "So do I, but you don't see me crying over an old glove or a scrap of writing like you do. And you can't say that I love her any less than the rest of her sisters." "Moreover, my dear girls," said Kenneth, taking his seat among them and lifting little Ernest onto his knee, "your spirits affect your father's. He feels the loss of his child, and you must all try to talk about her return, not her departure. I know how much you feel Kate's absence, but you must start looking at your separation as something that will happen one day. It is a natural part of life. There are three more who need to leave their home; how can you expect that all can be as fortunate as Blanche and Kate, who stay with you just as before? Paul's business will likely keep him away for a year, but he will return to settle here with us, and we must look at the bright side of things as long as we can. I've been telling Blanche, who's just as sensible as Lisa, all this, and now I'm here to ask you, for your own sake, to face unavoidable hardships with the strength that becomes so valuable once you've gained it. Minnie needs a scolding, I'm afraid," he continued, stroking her head affectionately. "Why don't you play the piano and sing as usual? The sound of music will lift our spirits, and the mechanical exercise of those little fingers will occupy your mind after a while, especially if you start working on those études by Moschelles, whose difficulty I have heard so much about." He smiled so encouragingly that Minnie hurried off to follow his advice, and soon after, Mr. de la Croix came out of his room, saying he was glad to hear the piano playing again. Minnie felt completely rewarded when she saw him return to his usual seat and fall asleep as she played; she confided to Kenneth that she was thankful for the scolding, but warned him not to tell Lisa, for she might take it the wrong way. That night, a long letter from Kate arrived, which helped to comfort them all. Poor Kate! Her return was meant to be a sorrowful one, as on the journey, her beautiful little girl, her darling Blanche, fell ill and quickly declined, leaving no hope by the time she arrived home. Silently, they cradled her in their arms and carried her to her own room, laying the little sufferer on the bed.

At that time, Fra Giovanni Agnolo, who was later appointed a Cardinal by Pope Paul III, felt a deep sense of gratitude towards Angelo, the General at Arezzo. Angelo had raised him and instilled in him a love for literature. In recognition of Angelo's influence, Agnolo crafted a stunning grey sandstone tomb for him in S. Piero, Arezzo. The tomb included detailed carvings, a realistic depiction of General Angelo on the sarcophagus, and two full-sized statues of crying boys representing the end of life's flame. Despite the tomb not being fully completed, Agnolo was summoned to Florence to assist with the city's festive preparations for the Emperor Charles V's victorious return from Tunis. Upon his arrival in Florence, Agnolo created an impressive eight-braccia figure of the River Arno on the Ponte a S. Trinita. The figure seemed to celebrate the Emperor's arrival alongside other rivers represented by statues crafted by other artists. Agnolo also made a twelve-braccia tall statue of Jason, the leader of the Argonauts, on the Canto de' Carnesecchi. However, because of its large size and limited time, this piece did not reach the same level of perfection as the Arno figure. Similarly, the figure of August Gladness he made on the Canto alla Cuculia did not meet the same acclaim. Although the time period was brief, Agnolo's works brought him significant recognition and fame from both craftsmen and the public. After completing his work in Arezzo, Agnolo learned that Girolamo Genga had a marble project in Urbino. However, when talks fell through, Agnolo went to Rome and then Naples, aiming to design the tomb for the respected poet, Jacopo Sannazzaro. Sannazzaro had built a beautiful residence at Margoglino, which he bequeathed to the Order of Servite Friars upon his death. He instructed his executors, Signor Cesare Mormerio and the Lord Count d'Aliffe, to build his tomb in the church he had built. The friars proposed Agnolo for the task, and after receiving a significant portion of the payment, he commissioned Francesco del Tadda of Fiesole to assist with the project. While preparing for the tomb, Agnolo was approached by four influential men appointed to fortify Naples against the advancing Turkish army. However, Agnolo, believing it inappropriate for a man of religion to engage in war-related work, informed the executors that he would complete the project either in Carrara or Florence. Agnolo then traveled to Florence, where he was commissioned by Signora Donna Maria, the mother of Duke Cosimo, to finish the S. Cosimo for the tomb of Lorenzo de' Medici. He also created a model for a Hercules statue to be placed atop a fountain at the Duke's villa at Castello. The model was well received, and Agnolo was told to quarry the marble in Carrara. While in Carrara, Agnolo received a letter from Cardinal Doria, who sought a sculptor to complete a statue of Prince Doria, initially assigned to Bandinelli. Despite Cardinal Cibo's efforts to send Agnolo to Genoa, Agnolo insisted on fulfilling his commitment to Duke Cosimo first. At this time, he made considerable progress on Sannazzaro's tomb and the Hercules statue. Upon returning to Florence, Agnolo worked diligently on the Hercules statue. However, rumors circulated that the marble was not as perfect as the model, and Agnolo faced difficulties fitting the legs to the torso. Messer Pier Francesco Riccio, the majordomo, began to withhold payments, influenced by Bandinelli's animosity towards Agnolo and the support of Tribolo, who was working on the Castello's ornaments. Feeling wronged, Agnolo departed for Genoa, where he obtained a commission to create a statue of Prince Doria from both the Cardinal Doria and the Prince. He finished the statue while continuing to supervise the work on Sannazzaro's tomb. The statue was well-received in Genoa, but Agnolo was disappointed when it was placed on the Piazza della Signoria instead of the Piazza Doria, as he had designed it to stand alone on a pedestal. In conclusion, where an artwork is placed greatly affects how it looks, since the artist takes into account lighting and viewing angles when creating it.

The Catholic University of Taiwan is known for founding the first graduate institute of philosophy in the region. The institution's new motto, "Truth, Goodness, Beauty, Sanctity," reflects its dedication to promoting intellectual growth and philosophical exploration. This vision played a key role in establishing the Fu Jen Philosophy Department, which became a prominent hub for Scholasticism in Taiwan. The department's standing was largely attributed to Yu Pin's influential philosophical ideas, especially his theory of the "Three Kinds of Knowing" (三知論). Over the six decades after World War II, the university's philosophical pursuits developed into a distinctive school of thought, deeply grounded in the traditions of Christian philosophy. The scholars at Fu Jen Catholic University have come to be recognized as part of the "Chinese Neo Scholastic Philosophy" group. This intellectual movement is known as the "Fu Jen School," reflecting the university's lasting impact on the field of philosophy. Notable members of this group include Bernard Li, Gabriel Chen, Ying Ly, Chien-ming Chu, and Hsiao Chih Sun. The university's scholarly work is also highlighted by its publication, "Universitas: Monthly Review of Philosophy and Culture," which is included in the Arts & Humanities Citation Index (A&HCI). Another key area of research at the institution is Fu Jen Religious Studies. For further exploration of related topics, one may refer to the Kyoto School, a Japanese intellectual movement that shares some philosophical similarities with the Fu Jen School. Additional resources and external links can provide a deeper understanding of Scholasticism and the philosophical traditions that have shaped the academic landscape at Fu Jen Catholic University.

In the 1980s, a wave of culturally and creatively progressive individuals arose, introducing innovative ideas that helped shape an alternative lifestyle. Larry Butler was a prominent figure among these visionaries. He worked as a caretaker at the Diorama, the first cinematic house in London, situated in Regent's Park. Butler was more than just a committed caretaker; he was also a trailblazer in communication, celebrated for his brilliance and forward-thinking leadership. The Diorama building became a hub for artists and performers in the late 1970s. They adopted a cooperative model across multiple areas such as arts, education, therapy, and disability arts, according to the website My Camden. From 1981 to 1992, the Diorama Arts Centre (DAC) experienced major transformations and faced considerable difficulties. On September 15, 1981, the Diorama Arts Centre was incorporated as both a charity and a company following a request from the Crown Estate Commissioners. In 1982, a formal lease agreement was put in place, replacing the earlier low peppercorn rent of about £25 annually. In 1983, the group risked being evicted as Greycoats Estates, representing the CEC, intended to redevelop the Diorama into office space. However, the Diorama Arts Centre fought against this attempted eviction and emerged victorious in 1984 after a public inquiry conducted by the Department of the Environment. The success was supported by the 'Re-use of Industrial Buildings Service' from URBED (Urbanism, Environment, and Design Ltd.). By February 1984, the Diorama Arts Trust was formed to propose a scheme that led to a £4 million fundraising effort, extending beyond 1984. CAST (Cartoon Archetypical Slogan Theatre), led by Roland Muldoon, also agreed to support the cause, further strengthening the movement.

The idea of desire and how it connects to will is truly intriguing. Desire can be seen as the root from which will grows, and over time, will can become independent and even surpass its original source. This is particularly evident in habitual actions, where individuals often continue to perform certain actions out of habit, even when the original motivation has faded. This phenomenon is not limited to virtuous actions but can also apply to neutral or even harmful behaviors that have become ingrained over time. The difference between will and desire is a key psychological reality. Will, like every part of our nature, can become habituated. We might end up wanting something not because we truly want it, but just because we've grown used to doing so. This is the power of habit, which can influence our actions even when they contradict our conscious preferences. In the case of virtue, a weak will can be strengthened by fostering a desire for it. By associating virtuous actions with pleasure and vice versa, we can evoke a will to be virtuous that, once established, operates independently of the original motivations of pleasure or pain. Will is born from desire but eventually comes under the influence of habit. Although habit's outcome isn't always good, the consistency it brings to our emotions and actions is essential for maintaining a reliable will to do what is right. The principle of utility, which holds that happiness or pleasure is the highest good, is closely connected to this conversation. If we accept that will is driven by desire and habit, and that these in turn are influenced by pleasure and pain, then the principle of utility gains support. However, whether this principle is valid remains for the reader to determine. Another intricate matter is the relationship between justice and utility. The strong sentiment associated with justice often leads people to view it as an absolute quality, distinct from the concept of expediency. Yet, the feeling of justice, like other instincts, may require guidance from a higher reason to ensure its appropriate application. The origin of the feeling of justice doesn't automatically justify every impulse it generates. Even if justice is an instinct, it may still need to be controlled and enlightened by reason. The subjective feeling of justice may be different from that of simple expediency, but this does not mean that justice cannot be seen as a part of general utility. To understand the nature of justice, it is essential to examine whether the feeling of justice and injustice is unique or derived from other feelings. If the feeling of justice is determined to result from other emotions, then its strength and nature could be explained by the general principles governing our emotional makeup. When looking for shared qualities between just and unjust actions, it's important to examine different examples. One common perception is that it is unjust to deprive someone of their personal liberty, property, or anything else that belongs to them by law. This belief, along with several others, will be examined more closely to uncover the fundamental characteristics that distinguish justice from injustice.

Sentimentalism, as a literary mode, has been a significant and recurring aspect of world literature, emphasizing emotions and feelings as the foundation of a person's actions and reactions, rather than reason. This literary movement encompasses various forms, including sentimental poetry, novels, and the German Empfindsamkeit music movement. European literary sentimentalism arose during the Age of Enlightenment, in part as a reaction to philosophical sentimentalism. In the 18th century, England witnessed the rise of the sentimental novel as a major literary genre. This development took place between 1730 and 1780, during the height of the Enlightenment, and subsequently spread to other European literatures. The philosophical underpinnings of sentimentalism primarily originated from Anthony Ashley Cooper, the 3rd Earl of Shaftesbury, who was a student of John Locke. Sentimentalism in both philosophy and literature can sometimes be challenging to differentiate, as they often influence and mirror each other. As philosophical ideas developed, literature began to adopt them by integrating them into stories and character portrayals. Consequently, it is common to observe the coexistence of both philosophical and literary movements. Philosophically, sentimentalism was often juxtaposed with rationalism. While 18th-century rationalism centered on cultivating an analytical mind as the foundation for discovering truth, sentimentalism highlighted the innate human ability for empathy, emotion, and moral sensitivity. This literary style aimed to delve into the richness of human feelings and the intricacies of relationships, offering a contrast to the prevailing rationalist perspective.

The French cavalry was famous for its skill, covering an impressive fifteen square miles of land. Each cavalry company had one hundred and twenty horses, mostly half-bred Percherons, with black and grey being the most common colors. A strong sense of competition existed between the companies, as each aimed to keep their teams in top condition. These teams were frequently portrayed in paintings, illustrating the men performing activities like chopping and sawing trees. John Nash, a well-known British painter, placed great emphasis on the significance of an artist's visual clarity and skilled hand movement. He believed that an artist's primary task is to train their eye to observe, probe, and then synchronize their hand movements with their visual perception. Nash's most famous war painting, "Over the Top," is an oil on canvas that measures 79.4 x 107.3 cm and is now on display at the Imperial War Museum in London. This painting depicts the 30th December 1917 Welsh Ridge counter-attack, when the 1st Battalion Artists Rifles (28th London Regiment) moved forward from their trenches toward Marcoing, near Cambrai. Tragically, out of the eighty men involved, sixty-eight were killed or wounded within the first few minutes of the attack. Nash was one of the twelve lucky survivors who endured the intense machine gun fire shown in the artwork. He finished this powerful piece three months after the event. "Over the Top" offers a stark and vivid depiction of soldiers moving into battle, fully aware of the high chance they won't come back alive. Nash's depiction conveys the raw emotion and harsh reality of war, as he recounts the experience of soldiers falling to the ground, some with screams and others in silence, as their comrades continue to push forward.

Examen philosophicum, which comes from the Latin term "philosophic exam" and is commonly abbreviated as Ex.phil., is one of the two main academic exams in most undergraduate programs at Norwegian universities. It is supported by the Examen facultatum, which emphasizes teaching students the skill of academic writing. In contrast, the Examen philosophicum is designed to develop students' grasp of philosophy and their capacity to think in an organized way. Examen philosophicum originated when it was first introduced at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark-Norway in 1675. However, it was stopped in Denmark in 1971, and its role in Norway has since decreased. The requirement for Examen philosophicum as a course is legally established through royal regulations unique to each university. For example, the 2005 Regulations No. 1798 on Studies and Exams at the University of Oslo, dated 20 December, provide the legal foundation for this requirement. Both the Examen philosophicum and Examen facultatum are essential parts of most bachelor's degree programs in Norway. Exceptions to this rule are mainly seen in professional studies at university colleges and a few natural science programs at universities, which might be exempt from one or both exams. The content of the Examen philosophicum can vary between universities and academic fields, often adjusted to match the scientific focus of each department and the specific area of study in the undergraduate program. For example, students specializing in foreign languages will follow a curriculum customarily designed to fit their particular field of study. The Examen philosophicum typically includes the study of philosophy, ethics, and rhetoric. The University of Oslo carried on the tradition of Examen philosophicum, implementing it in 1812, just two years after the university was founded. This exam remains an important part of Norway's higher education system, helping students develop critical thinking and a deeper understanding of philosophy.

As they traveled through the lush countryside of Hertfordshire and the green stretches of Warwickshire's coach roads, the man of the cloth observed a quiet shift in his companion, George Stobart. Though the scenery was beautiful and the sun felt pleasant, Stobart appeared lost in thought, his eyes fixed on some far-off place. The seasoned traveler, known for his punctuality and politeness, was also renowned for his wide sympathies. He had quickly assessed Stobart's character and found it to be of true mettle. Yet, he could not help but express his concern about the young man's apparent distraction. "I hope you do not begin to tire of your work, Stobart," he said, his voice filled with genuine concern. "I have seen many young men start with fervor, only to lose their way when faith wavers. But I do not believe you are one of them. However, I sense that something troubles you." "I am troubled, sir," Stobart admitted, his voice heavy with worry. "I am troubled by a soul I am trying to win for Christ, but with little success." The seasoned man, with a keen insight, guessed the source of Stobart's concern. "It is about your cousin's widow, Lady Kilrush, is it not?" he asked, his gaze piercing. "You have told me of her generous nature and her unconventional beliefs. I understand your desire to bring her into the fold, out of gratitude for her support of your work among the poor." Stobart was taken aback by the man's intuition. "Indeed, sir, you have guessed correctly. I have tried to reason with her, but her commanding temper and her dismissive manner make it difficult. It seems that the forces of darkness have the upper hand, and it is easier to deny than to prove. When I am with her, I find myself forgetting the spiritual danger she is in, even as she saves others from physical suffering." The wise man chided Stobart gently. "You have focused too much on the woman and not enough on her soul. Her beauty has blinded your judgment. As your mentor and friend, I warn you against cherishing the company of a beautiful heathen unless your sole intent is her salvation." Stobart was quick to defend himself. "I assure you, sir, I have never entertained an unworthy thought about Lady Kilrush. She has always treated me with sisterly affection. Her beauty does not alter my concern for her soul. I would give half my life to save her from the dangers of worldly pleasures and the company of the unscrupulous." "If you can keep your conscience clear and win this woman from the clutches of Satan, you will have done well," the wise man advised. "But do not compromise the truth. If you fail to guide her towards righteousness, you must part ways with her forever." The conversation took a personal turn as the wise man shared his own experiences. "You know, Stobart, I too have known the pain of unrequited love. The woman I loved before Mrs. Wesley was a domestic servant, yet her intellect and character were worthy of the highest esteem. Circumstances kept us apart, and I chose someone else." His voice faded into a sigh, betraying the depth of his unsaid grief. Stobart spent a month on the road with his mentor, preaching in Bristol and to the miners of Kingswood. They traveled from south to north, accompanied by one of Wesley's earliest and most gifted lay preachers. This unassuming man, though born into humble circumstances, was a compelling speaker, able to move the hearts of those who had never encountered the teachings of God. The journey was filled with hardships and inconveniences, but the travelers bore them with good humor, inspired by Wesley's cheerful spirit and Christian contentment. By the time they reached London in May, Stobart had been away for over a month. He got weekly letters from his wife, describing her household worries and their child's development. He, in turn, wrote to her about his adventures, knowing she took great interest in the fine houses he visited and the social customs he observed. Their marriage, though devoid of the initial fervor of romantic love, was one of tranquil affection and mutual respect. Stobart believed he had chosen well in marrying the printer's daughter, as she allowed him the freedom to pursue his spiritual journey. During the religious pilgrimage, Stobart had written several letters to Lady Kilrush, inspired by his conversations with Wesley and his spiritual experiences. Richard Hamilton's iconic pop art collage, first created in black and white, has been widely recognized and used. It was also included in posters for an exhibition highlighting the artwork. Hamilton has returned to and reworked the subject and composition of his original collage in different forms, including a 1992 version that features a female bodybuilder. Hamilton's work has inspired many artists to produce derivative pieces. Photomontage, the technique Hamilton used in his collage, includes a range of methods for merging images. This method involves Victorian "combination printing," in which several negatives are printed onto one sheet of paper, as shown by O. G. Rejlander. G. Rejlander demonstrated this technique in 1857. Other approaches involve front-projection and computer-generated montage techniques. Artists like Romare Bearden have also employed photomontage in their work. Bearden's process involved creating compositions with paper, paint, and photographs on small boards, which he then fixed with an emulsion applied using a hand roller. These collages were subsequently enlarged through photographic means. Combining several images into a single composite and then photographing the final result was a common technique in press photography and offset lithography throughout the 19th century. This practice persisted until the advent of digital image editing, which has revolutionized the process of creating photomontages. Today, magazine photo editors frequently utilize digital tools to produce "paste-ups." The development of computer software, like Adobe Photoshop and Pixelmator, has greatly streamlined the creation of photomontages, making them more accessible to a wider array of artists and designers.

Metanarrative, also known as a "master narrative" or "totalizing narrative," refers to a comprehensive and overarching explanation or framework that seeks to provide a coherent understanding of the historical record. It is a broad narrative that strives to account for events, developments, and phenomena within a specific context or across different contexts. The concept of metanarrative has been widely discussed and debated in various fields, including philosophy, sociology, and literary theory. It is often associated with the idea of a grand narrative that encompasses all aspects of human experience and knowledge, aiming to offer a unified perspective on the world. In the context of history, a metanarrative might refer to a prevailing story or explanation that influences how people interpret and comprehend past events. For example, a metanarrative could be a belief in the inevitability of progress, the triumph of reason over superstition, or the continuous struggle between different social classes. However, the idea of metanarrative has also been criticized for its potential to oversimplify complex realities and to suppress alternative perspectives. Critics argue that metanarratives can be limiting and exclusionary, as they often fail to account for the diversity and nuance of human experiences. In response to these concerns, some scholars have advocated for a move away from metanarratives towards a more fragmented and pluralistic approach to understanding history and culture. This approach emphasizes the importance of recognizing and valuing multiple narratives and perspectives, rather than seeking a single, all-encompassing explanation. In short, the idea of a metanarrative is intricate and layered, shaping the way we comprehend and make sense of the world. While it can offer a sense of coherence and order, it also raises important questions about the nature of knowledge, power, and representation.

Ibn al-Haytham, a renowned medieval scholar, advocated for a critical and self-reflective approach to scientific inquiry. He emphasized the importance of avoiding personal biases and maintaining an objective stance during the examination of scientific theories. This skepticism and methodical approach to experimentation can be traced back to his Islamic faith, which taught him that humans are inherently flawed while only God is perfect. Ibn al-Haytham believed that to truly understand the nature of the universe, it is essential to eliminate human error and opinion, allowing the natural world to reveal its own truths. In his work *The Winding Motion*, he contrasted the Islamic prophetic tradition with the demonstrative sciences, emphasizing the differing approaches to applying faith in each field. He claimed that faith in the prophetic tradition is similar to blindly accepting Ptolemy's statements without looking for proof or evidence, which is not how mathematicians in the demonstrative sciences proceed. Ibn al-Haytham saw his quest for knowledge and truth as a spiritual path that drew him nearer to God. He stated, "I constantly sought knowledge and truth, and it became my belief that for gaining access to the effulgence and closeness to God, there is no better way than that of searching for truth and knowledge." His contemporary, Abū Rayhān al-Bīrūnī, also contributed significantly to the early development of scientific methodology, further emphasizing the importance of critical thinking and empirical evidence in the pursuit of knowledge.

Environmental history is the study of the complex interactions between human societies and the natural environment. It examines how particular species and landscapes can be domesticated, which may affect the development of human culture and even guide its course. Two contrasting viewpoints exist within this field: environmental determinism and cultural determinism. Environmental determinism suggests that historical development is mainly influenced by environmental conditions instead of cultural factors. Conversely, cultural determinism argues that human influence is so pervasive that the concept of pristine nature holds little validity. From this perspective, interacting with nature inevitably involves a cultural framework. Many scholars have offered important insights into how to approach environmental history research. Donald Worster, Carolyn Merchant, William Cronon, and Ian Simmons have all made significant contributions to the field. Worster's framework, which includes three core subject areas— the environment itself, human impacts on the environment, and human thought about the environment— serves as a foundational starting point for students. This approach requires a diverse skill set and fluency in the language of natural science, particularly ecology. Environmental history naturally involves multiple disciplines, incorporating methods and perspectives from both the physical and social sciences. There is broad consensus on the value of combining knowledge from different disciplines to achieve a full understanding of the connection between people and the environment. Some key works in the field of environmental history include: - Chakrabarti, Ranjan (ed.), "Does Environmental History Matter: Shikar, Subsistence, Sustenance and the Sciences" (Kolkata: Readers Service, 2006) This edited volume, compiled by Ranjan Chakrabarti, delves into various aspects of environmental history, emphasizing its significance and relevance in understanding the intricate relationship between humans and their surroundings.

Post-Impressionism and Fauvism were important artistic movements that shaped a group of Chilean artists, who also found inspiration in other styles like Expressionism and Cubism, though to a smaller degree. This group opposed the academic art and the romantic Criollismo that dominated Chile during that period. The group included notable artists such as Pablo Burchard (1875–1964), Jorge Caballero (1902–1992), Isaías Cabezón (1891–1963), Hector Cáceres (1897–1980), Ana Cortés (1906–1998), Augusto Eguiluz (1893–1969), Jorge Letelier (1887–1966), Camilo Mori (1896–1973), Julio Ortiz de Zárate Pinto (1885–1943), Manuel Ortiz de Zárate Pinto (1887–1946), Henriette Petit (1894–1983), José Perotti (1898–1956), Inés Puyó (1906–1996), Luis Vargas Rosas (1897–1977), Pablo Vidor (1892–1991), Waldo Vila (1894–1979), Marta Villanueva (1900–1995), and Álvaro Yáñez Bianchi, known as "Juan Emar" (1893–1964). The "40 Generation" is a group of artists who graduated in 1940 and became well-known following their exhibition at the Salón Oficial in 1941. This exhibition was a contest organized by the executive committee of the Museum of Fine Arts, open to both Chilean and foreign artists as long as their works were created in Chile. The contest began each year on November 15th during the Chilean spring. The 40 Generation is known for their love of Impressionism and Fauvism, along with their skill in drawing and creating harmonious compositions. They are also notable for keeping a distance from the political unrest that was prevalent in the country at the time. This artistic movement marked a major change in the Chilean art scene, showing a push for innovation and a move away from traditional artistic norms.

"Can wisdom's magic force truly repel? It beckons the revered hermit from his sanctuary. It was dusk, as poets wittily recount, when Phoebus, the sun, descended into Thetis' embrace: she blushed, then extinguished the light, drawing the modest veils of night. To be honest, the sun had set by the time our tired travelers arrived in town. They sought refuge in a lordly mansion, a testament to pride and luxury. The courteous courtier hesitated at the threshold, reluctant to enter, yet by command, he obeyed and stepped within. In a spacious room adorned with rich tapestries, they paused to rest their weary limbs, awaiting the silence that would invite them to feast. As Cynthia's silver light touched the pale horizon, the company, having finished their varied supper, retired to a distant room, leaving behind servants and all, to indulge in a ball. The host guided his guests to a place set up to fulfill their noble aspirations. Plates still half-full lined the table, with tempting bits scattered on the floor. The courteous mouse offered the best, and both reveled in the abundance. The industrious peasant roamed, grateful for life's fortunate turn. In the heart of a bountiful pie, they lay sated and carefree. Yet, the cruel hand of fate turned, revealing the storms that await mortal splendor. With a loud noise, the servants and dogs stormed into the room, driving the gluttons away in fear, as they cursed their own fullness, which hindered their escape. The shivering peasant yearned for the refuge of rocks and mountains, regretting the very life he had once condemned. "This life," he cried, "is surely the worst. Grant me again, gods, my cave and woods; let peace and simple fare be my sustenance." Horace to Fuscus Aristius, in a paraphrase of the Eightieth Epistle of the First Book of Horace, extols the virtues of health and the contrasting lifestyles of the city and country. The country dweller finds comfort in nature's arms, free from the city's manufactured pleasures. He questions the allure of luxury, suggesting that nature's bounty and tranquility offer true contentment. The man who swaps gold for brass or real gems for glass, he argues, is just as foolish as someone who exchanges real goods for the empty show of pride and vanity. He advises his friend to value the wealth he has and to control his cravings, cautioning that seeking more brings only mockery and misery. In "The Country Life," the author celebrates the simple pleasures of a modest field and garden, free from the ostentatious inconveniences of a life of business and state. He tells the story of Abdolonymus, who reluctantly traded his tranquil cottage for a throne, frequently casting longing glances backward. The tale of Aglaüs, a humble man whose happiness was recognized by the gods, further illustrates the virtues of a simple life. The author yearns for a quiet existence, tending to his own small plot of land, free from the burdens of wealth and power. He begs the gods to allow him this peaceful retreat, where he can find comfort in the simple pleasures of life. In "The Garden," the author expresses his lifelong desire for a small house with a large garden, a place where he can cultivate not only plants but also the tranquility and contentment that come from living in harmony with nature.

Tarzan the Fearless, which came out in 1933, started the Tarzan film series. It first premiered as a 12-part serial and was later released as an edited feature film with the same name. The film featured Buster Crabbe, who won a gold medal in swimming at the 1932 Olympics. Crabbe's portrayal of Tarzan was the first under the production of Sol Lesser, who would later become the franchise's producer when it moved to RKO. After playing Tarzan, Crabbe continued his career with success in B-films and television, including roles as space opera heroes Flash Gordon and Buck Rogers. In 1935, The New Adventures of Tarzan was released, which brought the character back to his original concept as an intelligent Englishman. This serial also included Herman Brix, another Olympian recognized for his accomplishments in shotput. The serial was reedited into two feature films: the first came out the same year under the same title, and the second, *Tarzan and the Green Goddess*, was released in 1938. Edgar Rice Burroughs, the creator of the Tarzan character, had a financial interest in the production. Brix later renamed himself Bruce Bennett and went on to have a lengthy career in both film and television. Tarzan's Revenge, released in 1938, starred Glenn Morris, a gold medal winner in the Olympic decathlon in 1936. His performance was featured in part two of Leni Riefenstahl's film Olympia. Morris was the fourth Olympian to portray Tarzan. Co-starring with him was Eleanor Holm, an Olympic swimmer who won gold in 1932 but was controversially expelled from the 1936 Olympics. She portrayed a Jane-like character named Eleanor. This film was also produced by Sol Lesser. However, Tarzan's Revenge received poor reviews, which impacted Morris's acting career.

Gottlob Frege, a German philosopher, logician, and mathematician, made significant contributions to the development of predicate logic with his work "Begriffsschrift" (English: Concept-script, 1879). This innovative work broadened the scope of logical analysis, enabling more sentences to be translated into logical form and going beyond the constraints of traditional Aristotelian logic. In the late 19th century, German philosophy was heavily shaped by Neo-Kantianism. Unlike the widespread psychologism of the era, Edmund Husserl's 1891 book "Philosophie der Arithmetik" argued that the idea of cardinal numbers arises from mental acts of grouping and counting objects. Frege, however, presented a different perspective in his works "The Foundations of Arithmetic" (1884) and "The Basic Laws of Arithmetic" (German: "Grundgesetze der Arithmetik," 1893–1903). He claimed that mathematics and logic have their own public objects, separate from the private beliefs or mental states of individual mathematicians and logicians, similar to the ideas of Plato or Bernard Bolzano. Following Frege, the logicists began to advocate a form of mathematical platonism. Frege's influence extended beyond mathematics and logic, as he also played a pivotal role in the philosophy of language and the development of analytic philosophy's focus on meaning. Michael Dummett attributes the linguistic turn in analytic philosophy to Frege's "Foundations of Arithmetic" and his context principle. Frege's influential 1892 paper "On Sense and Reference" presented his famous puzzles and laid out his theory of mediated reference, which has continued to shape the study of meaning in language. His 1918 paper "The Thought: A Logical Inquiry" further illustrated his opposition to idealism and psychologism, as well as his focus on language, by promoting a platonist view of propositions or thoughts. In short, Gottlob Frege's contributions to predicate logic, the philosophy of mathematics, and the philosophy of language have made a significant and enduring impact across many areas of study, influencing the development of contemporary philosophical and mathematical ideas.

The Rothschild Publishing House, originally known as Dr. Walther Rothschild Verlagsbuchhandlung, was established in 1905 and quickly gained a reputation as a respected publisher in the fields of cultural studies, political philosophy, and the philosophy of law. The publishing house was renowned for its meticulous attention to detail in editing and its proficiency in organization, which contributed to its success. The fundamental philosophy of the Rothschild Publishing House is eloquently captured in the words spoken during the celebration of its 25th anniversary in 1930: "The work of the scholar prospers in solitude. Relying solely on their own intellectual prowess, scholars strive to deduce the laws of the world and find formulations that hold true. For the scientific person, the quest for complete knowledge brings a sense of joy and satisfaction. Initially, the general public may be indifferent to this internal process. However, the private sphere is breached when the publisher transforms these thoughts into a broader context, turning a manuscript into a book. In doing so, ideas are disseminated to the world, and the printed work imparts results and new tasks to the scientific community, creating intellectual currents that connect different times and countries." Historian Walter Rothschild (1879–1967), who earned his Doctor of Philosophy degree in 1902, was the owner and a leading figure of the Dr. Walther Rothschild Publishing House. His expertise and dedication to the field played a significant role in shaping the publishing house's reputation and contributions to academia.

The relentless assault of the elements was a constant challenge, with the air sometimes crackling with the force of exploding bolts. It was a profound relief when the sick and injured were finally freed from this elemental turmoil, which Stanley described as more terrifying than any European battle. His men seemed almost unable to function due to a mix of fear, pain, sickness, the loss of friends, hunger, rain, thunder, and a pervasive feeling of hopelessness. They sought refuge under banana trees, behind the shields of the indigenous people, under woolen covers, straw mats, and even beneath earthen and copper pots. Each man was surrounded by a blue haze of desolation, completely overcome by a silent terror. The sight of the tired donkeys, with their ears pinned back, eyes shut, and heads low, along with the birds in cages whose feathers were all out of order, only intensified the overall sense of despair. Hunger, sickness, and wounds inflicted by the thorns in the woods incapacitated many, and the threat of poisoned arrows from hidden savages loomed large. Carriers would vanish, taking their precious loads with them, and each day saw more men felled by exhaustion, never to rise again. Despite the unbearable hardship, the call was always "forward, forward." On the rare occasions when rain ceased, an eerie darkness settled over the forest. The travelers encountered slippery tree trunks that served as bridges over treacherous chasms, threatening to impale them with the sharp points of their protruding dead branches as they careened down the hillsides. They had to cross a fast-moving stream, carefully balancing on its smooth, wet surface. Soon they were trapped in a thicket, almost suffocating under the thick tangle of vines and bushes that wrapped around them. They trudged through a morass, its perilous depths hidden beneath a layer of floating plants and scum. With each step, their difficulties multiplied, until Stanley finally declared that they had pushed far enough for the day and decided to make camp. Stanley was moved by compassion as he observed his followers, their once ebony skin now ashen gray, their bones protruding so starkly that it was a wonder they had the strength to continue. Yet he offered no mercy, pushing them forward with strict discipline out of fear that the expedition would fail. He knew that to linger was to court death. The soil was soaked with decaying vegetation, the air thick and stifling, heavy with the smells of rotting insects, leaves, plants, twigs, and stalks. At every turn, they were ensnared by tenacious vines, thorns, poisonous ivies, or monstrous thistles, which tore at them as they struggled to free themselves. The sheer number of insects made their situation worse, particularly the black ants that fell from the trees, their stings even more painful than those of wasps or red ants. These ants advanced in organized groups along the trails, and the plants and animals were filled with them. By November, the expedition had been halved, with only two hundred men emerging from the gloom of the forest into the clear light of day. In his account of the journey, Stanley expressed gratitude for the absence of the larger African fauna, but this was not always the case. The wilderness was full of elephants, buffaloes, panthers, leopards, jackals, antelopes, and gazelles. The rivers housed hippos and snakes, the trees were filled with numerous birds, and the woods sheltered a wide range of monkeys. None of these creatures encountered the expedition. The same applied to the natives. They frequently came across cleared areas where bananas and pisangs were grown, as well as the deserted huts of the savages who ran away when strangers approached. However, it would be incorrect to assert that the forests were devoid of human presence. Behind every tree, an enemy lurked, and their poisoned arrows frequently found their mark. Stanley insisted that these forest dwellers were far more perilous than the open country's inhabitants. It was remarkable that, amidst the myriad dangers they faced, they managed to avoid a conflict that could have been catastrophic. The terrible dangers of the forest gradually faded away. On November 30th, the expedition arrived at a wide, well-kept road that climbed toward the top of a charming hill. Lights were visible in the distance. The people gathered on the slope, their questioning glances betraying their disbelief and hope: "Is it true? Are we deceived? Is it possible that we have emerged from those forest terrors?" They were soon convinced, and a few moments later, they gazed in awe and wonder at the vista before them. Longingly, they stretched out their arms towards the beautiful landscape. All looked up with thankful hearts to the clear, blue sky and watched the sun set as if under a spell.

Tully once posited that drama should serve as a mirror reflecting human life, a model of proper conduct, and a representation of truth. However, the plays we witness today are quite the opposite, often reflecting nonsense, folly, and lewdness. Consider the absurdity of a character appearing as an infant in swaddling clothes in one scene, only to reappear as a bearded adult in the next. Equally preposterous is the portrayal of an elderly man as a dashing hero, a young man as a coward, a servant speaking eloquently, a page offering wise counsel, a king working as a porter, or a princess toiling as a kitchen maid. The lack of attention to historical accuracy in these plays is just as serious. I have seen a play where the first act unfolds in Europe, the second in Asia, and the third concludes in Africa. If it had been a four-act play, no doubt the final act would have taken place in America, covering all corners of the globe. How can we expect an audience to suspend disbelief when the play is set during the reign of King Pepin or Charlemagne, yet features Emperor Heraclius, who lived centuries later? Blending historical facts with fiction in a way that lacks even a hint of plausibility or accuracy is completely unacceptable. Sadly, some people consider this a form of perfection, dismissing any attempt at refinement as pretentious. Sacred dramas are not spared from this travesty, with playwrights inventing miracles and attributing them to the wrong saints. Even secular plays introduce miracles or transformations without any logical reason, merely to astonish and attract audiences. This trend not only distorts the truth and corrupts history but also tarnishes the reputation of Spanish playwrights. Foreigners, who strictly follow the rules of drama, see us as barbaric and ignorant when they observe the absurdity of our plays. It is insufficient to argue that the primary purpose of public performances is to provide harmless entertainment and prevent the vices of idleness. A well-crafted play can better accomplish this objective, entertaining the audience while also enlightening and inspiring them morally. The poets themselves aren't completely at fault. Some are aware of their shortcomings and know how to improve, but they cater to the demands of actors who are willing to pay for plays that fit their preferences. This has led to the creation of countless plays that, despite their brilliance, grace, and eloquence, fail to reach their full potential. Some playwrights compose works so boldly that actors must escape following shows, worried about retribution for angering royalty or nobility. These issues could be resolved if an intelligent and sensible person were appointed to review all plays before they are performed, ensuring their quality and adherence to the rules of drama. As the canon and the curate kept talking, the barber came up and proposed a place where they could rest and let their oxen graze. The canon, intrigued by the curate and eager to learn more about Don Quixote, decided to join them for the afternoon. He had his servants go get supplies from the nearby inn, but they found that their own pack mule already had enough food for everyone. Meanwhile, Sancho Panza, seeking a moment alone with his master, approached Don Quixote's cage and revealed his suspicions about the true identities of the curate and the barber. He believed they were behind the enchantment that had befallen Don Quixote.

The Constructivist movement, from 1921 to 1924, produced works that anticipated the "shaped canvas" paintings, which became prominent after 1945. These early examples of shaped canvases were showcased extensively during the 1920s. Notable exhibitions featured two collaborative shows with László Moholy-Nagy at the Der Sturm Gallery in Berlin in 1922 and 1923, along with the International Exhibition of Modern Art, organized by the Societe Anonyme, at the Brooklyn Museum in New York in 1926. Abraham Joel Tobias, an artist famous for his shaped canvases, kept producing similar works during the 1930s. In a similar vein, Uruguayan artist Rhod Rothfuss started experimenting with "irregular frame" paintings in 1942. In late 1944, he released a groundbreaking essay entitled "El marco: un problema de la plástica actual" in the Arturo magazine, continuing to delve into the idea of shaped canvases. Munich-born painter Rupprecht Geiger also played a role in shaping the development of shaped canvases, showcasing his work in Paris, France, in 1948. New Orleans-born abstract painter Edward Clark became known for his shaped canvas paintings, which were exhibited at New York's Brata Gallery in 1957. During the late 1950s through the mid-1960s, Jasper Johns investigated the use of shaped and compartmentalized canvases in his work, most famously in his "Three Flags" piece, which featured a smaller canvas placed on top of a larger one. Another key artist, Robert Rauschenberg, explored divided and shaped canvases in his assemblages and "combines" throughout the 1950s. Argentine artist Lucio Fontana experimented with shaped and compartmentalized canvases through his Concetto Spaziale, Attese series, which he began in 1959. While determining a precise starting point for postwar shaped canvas painting might be difficult, it's clear that the idea had already taken shape by the late 1940s and kept developing throughout the mid-20th century, with many artists helping to shape and spread its influence.

Facing the narrow pass, choosing to move forward or back was filled with danger. The infantry, congesting the road behind, hindered movement, while the relentless barrage of rocks and logs cascading down the slope wreaked havoc, tearing through the ranks and casting men and horses into the waters below. The onslaught endured for a brief spell until the collective resolve broke, and the majority turned their horses, seeking the safety of the rear. In the ensuing chaos, many were pushed over the edge to meet their end in the depths of the lake. The main force, in its panicked flight, collided with its own infantry, trampling the unfortunate souls underfoot in a desperate bid to escape. The Swiss, having dispatched the remaining knights at the forefront, descended upon the rear of the disorganized horde, cutting down both horsemen and foot soldiers with ease, as there was little to no resistance. John of Winterthur, a chronicler of the time, described the scene not as a battle, but a brutal massacre, with the Swiss slaughtering the duke's men mercilessly, offering no mercy until none were left to kill. The Swiss secured their freedom by employing instinctive tactical prowess, denying the feudal cavalry any advantageous position to launch an attack. They controlled the battlefield, dictating where the fighting would occur. The Austrians, unable to gain momentum on the steep and slippery terrain or utilize their numerical superiority due to the narrowness of the pass, were rendered impotent. However, the extent of the defeat was primarily caused by Duke Leopold's unacceptable negligence, as he had failed to explore the path and had fallen into the deadly trap of the pass. The Battle of Morgarten revealed the early stages of the Swiss military system. Though the Confederate victories were achieved through the charge of a column, it was the halberd, not the pike, that was the instrument of their triumph. The pike was not yet widely adopted among the mountaineers of the three cantons, and in fact, was never as prevalent among them as it was among the Swiss of the lower Alpine regions and the Aar valley, the Bernese, and the people of Zurich and Lucerne. The halberd, despite its lethality, was not a weapon that would grant an absolute advantage to its bearers. It was the positioning, not the weapons or tactics, that led to the Swiss victory at Morgarten. However, their second major victory at Laupen carries even more military importance. It was here that, for the first time since the Roman era, infantry, without cavalry support, held their ground on open plains against a larger force fully armed. It was twenty-four years after Duke Leopold's defeat when the Confederates, along with their newly allied Bernese brethren, confronted the Burgundian nobility's forces, assembled by all the feudal lords between Alsace and Lake Geneva. Count Gerard of Vallangin, leading the baronial army, intended to determine the outcome by outflanking and overpowering one side of the enemy. For this purpose, he placed all his cavalry on the right flank, while his center and left were made up entirely of infantry. The Swiss adopted the three-column formation that would become their standard battle order. Under the unified command of Rudolf of Erlach, who is credited with first employing this formation, the Bernese, primarily armed with pikes, formed the central column, with the flanks drawn back. The left wing consisted of men from the three old cantons, who still used the halberd as their primary weapon, whereas the right was made up of other Bernese allies. In this formation, they advanced to the attack, with the center column significantly ahead. The baronial infantry could not stand against the Confederates, as the Bernese steadily forced them back, crushing the front lines and pushing the rest off the battlefield. Shortly afterwards, the Burgundian left met the same outcome at the hands of the Swiss right column. Without pausing to pursue, the two victorious groups turned to assist the men of the Forest Cantons, who were surrounded by a relentless onslaught of horsemen. Although the halberd was capable of causing severe injuries, it couldn't completely stop the cavalry from sometimes getting close. Yet, the mountaineers stood firm, withstanding the relentless attacks until the enemy infantry had been driven off the field. Then, the two successful columns struck the left and rear of the baronial cavalry, meeting their charge head-on. It appears the enemy had already been weakened by their previous failed efforts to conquer the Forest Cantons, as after a single unsuccessful attempt to charge the Bernese pikemen, they turned and fled, suffering heavy losses as many of their rear units were cut off and forced into the river Sense. Although Laupen was not as bloody or dramatic as Morgarten, it was one of three key battles that marked the beginning of a new era in military history.

In the tale of Hiawatha, the land was once plagued by a band of black marauders, who mocked the wise man Hiawatha with their melancholic laughter, shaking the treetops with their mirth. They scorned his words and his plans, but Hiawatha, ever watchful and thoughtful, had heard their ridicule from the treetops. As the quiet night wrapped around the fields and woods, the sad Wawonaissa sang among the hemlocks, and the Spirit of Sleep, Nepahwin, shut the doors of the wigwams. From her bed, Laughing Water got up, shed her clothes, and, without fear, wandered through the cornfields, tracing a sacred, magical circle with her footprints to safeguard them. Only the midnight hour and the Wawonaissa saw her actions, keeping her beauty hidden and unspoken of. With the dawn, Kahgahgee, the King of Ravens, rallied his flock of crows, blackbirds, jays, and ravens to descend upon Hiawatha's fields, intent on desecrating the grave of Mondamin. However, Hiawatha, having anticipated this, had set snares across the cornfields and lay in wait, ready to ambush the birds. Unaware of the danger, the marauders were quickly ensnared by Hiawatha's traps. Emerging from his hiding place, Hiawatha struck terror into the hearts of the birds with his fearsome appearance. He cruelly killed many, displaying their dead bodies on poles to warn the others. Only Kahgahgee was left alive, captured as a hostage to guarantee the good behavior of his people. As summer faded and Shawondasee's warmth spread across the land, the cornfields reached their peak in beauty. Nokomis, an elder, suggested to Minnehaha that it was time to harvest the maize. Laughing Water, along with Nokomis and others, gathered the community for the harvest, while the old men and warriors watched from the shade of the pine trees, enjoying the lively labor and the merriment of the young people. When a red maize-ear was found, it was a sign of future love, and when a blighted one was discovered, it led to jests and imitations of the elderly, filling the air with laughter. Hiawatha mourned the temporary nature of memory and the disappearance of traditions, accomplishments, and knowledge. He observed that the grave-posts of their ancestors bore no markings, leaving the deceased without recognition or identity. To remedy this, he created a system of picture-writing, using symbols to convey meaning and preserve knowledge for future generations. He painted various figures on the bark of a birch tree, each with a specific significance. The Great Spirit was shown as an egg with points reaching toward the four directions, symbolizing presence everywhere. The Spirit of Evil was a serpent, representing cunning and deceit. Life and death were circles, the sun, moon, stars, and various creatures of the earth were also painted, along with symbols for the earth and sky, day and night, sunrise, sunset, and noon. Hiawatha taught his people the meanings of these symbols and encouraged them to adorn their grave-posts with ancestral totems and household symbols, ensuring that future generations could identify and remember their lineage. In this way, Hiawatha's ingenuity and foresight not only protected the cornfields from the black marauders but also preserved his people's knowledge and heritage through the art of picture-writing.

The character "Prometheus," played by Spencer Wilding and Guillaume Delaunay, appears in multiple film adaptations. In 2015, Bernard Rose directed a modern adaptation of *Frankenstein* that centers on the Monster's intelligence and his organic creation via DNA manipulation, instead of the conventional method of reanimating corpses. The story is told from the Monster's point of view, providing a new interpretation of the original novel. In 2019, Larry Fessenden wrote and directed *Depraved*, a modern retelling focused on a soldier suffering from PTSD who brings life into a Brooklyn loft. Looking forward to 2024, Guillermo del Toro will be writing and directing a fresh adaptation of the novel, offering yet another distinctive take on this enduring tale. Besides these adaptations, "Frankenstein" has also led to many parodies and satires. Between 1921 and 1922, H.P. Lovecraft penned the serialized "Herbert West, Reanimator," a satirical homage to Mary Shelley's original work. The 1942 Mighty Mouse cartoon, "Frankenstein's Cat," shows a group of mice and birds living peacefully until a mechanical cat with a relentless hunger upsets their harmony. The 1964 cartoon "Dr. Devil and Mr. Hare" features a Frankenstein monster robot that battles both the Tasmanian Devil and Bugs Bunny. A 1965-1968 cartoon series introduced the overly-nice Milton the Monster and "Fangenstein." Dr. Frankenstein and his Monster also appeared in the animated film "Mad Monster Party." Over the years, "Frankenstein" has continued to captivate audiences with its themes of creation, morality, and the consequences of playing with the forces of life and death. Every adaptation and parody provides a distinct viewpoint, guaranteeing the lasting impact of this classic tale.

The Spanish Era, also referred to as the Era of Caesar, was a calendar system used for numbering years that was prevalent on the Iberian Peninsula from the 5th century through the 15th century. It was eventually replaced by the Anno Domini (AD) system. The beginning of the Spanish Era, or its starting point, was January 1, 38 BC. To convert a year from the Anno Domini calendar to the Spanish Era, you add 38 to the AD year. For instance, the year 941 in the Spanish Era corresponds to AD 903. When dates were written in the Spanish Era, the word "era" was consistently followed by a feminine ordinal number, which contrasted with the masculine "anno" (year) used in the AD system. For example, the Spanish Era would express the year as "era millesima octava," whereas the AD system would use "anno millesimo octavo." The precise reasons for selecting 38 BC as the beginning of the Spanish Era remain unknown. One theory proposes that it might have been influenced by an Easter table that started in that year. Another possibility is that it was connected to the general tax imposed by Caesar Augustus and the mapping of the Roman world, as noted by Isidore of Seville in his "Etymologiae," written in the early 7th century. Isidore of Seville explained the meaning of the Latin word "aera," which is the plural of "aes," referring to bronze, brass, or copper. He claimed that the term "era" was introduced by Caesar Augustus when he initially imposed a general tax and surveyed the Roman world. The term "aera" was used because it was believed that the whole world would supply copper to the state. However, it is important to note that the actual meaning of "period of time" associated with "aera" originates from the use of bronze counters in calculations. The Spanish Era played a significant role in the historical calendar system of the Iberian Peninsula and offers important insights into the region's cultural and historical background.

During the Middle Helladic period, communities like Lerna showed unique features in their settlement arrangements and everyday life. Approximately two-thirds of the graves discovered within these communities were cist graves, indicating a common burial practice. Towns were frequently built around a central cist, implying that this burial method held cultural or religious importance. Settlements during this time had an irregular layout, with houses closely clustered together in a seemingly random arrangement. It is believed that the way homes were arranged was due to the wish to live near relatives or people from the same social group or faction. Housing structures were usually single-story, U-shaped buildings constructed from clay. A typical house would include a porch, up to three rooms, an inner chamber with a hearth, and designated spaces for storage and cooking. A larger, standalone house has been found, thought to have been the home of a chief or community leader. This structure featured a separate storage facility and a courtyard with a hearth, reflecting the elevated status of its occupant. Agriculture was essential to the economy of the Middle Helladic period. People grew a wide range of crops, such as wheat, which was turned into flour for bread, barley, flax, peas, chickpeas, lentils, and beans.
