In summary, long-term potentiation, kindling, and central sensitization are interconnected processes that contribute to our understanding of learning, memory, epilepsy, and chronic pain. These phenomena highlight the complex nature of the brain's response to repeated stimuli and the potential for lasting changes in neural function.

Max Weber was a well-known sociologist whose work was deeply shaped by Karl Marx's ideas. However, he differed from Marx by dismissing the viability of a successful communist system. Weber contended that communism would necessitate a higher degree of social control and bureaucracy than what is present in capitalist societies. He also criticized Marx's idea of a proletarian revolution, considering it unlikely. Weber put forward a three-component theory of stratification and introduced the idea of life chances. He thought there were more class distinctions than Marx had proposed, combining ideas from both functionalist and Marxist perspectives into his own theoretical framework. Weber highlighted the difference between class, status, and power, viewing them as distinct yet related forms of influence that shape social behavior in different ways. Unlike Marx, who operated in the 19th century, Weber, who came to work fifty years later, identified four main social classes: the upper class, white-collar workers, the petite bourgeoisie, and the manual working class. His main ideas about social stratification came from analyzing the social structure in Germany. Weber observed that stratification was not solely based on the ownership of capital, as Marx had theorized. He pointed out cases in which aristocrats did not possess substantial economic wealth yet held considerable political influence. In contrast, certain affluent families had limited status and authority because of elements like their Jewish background. In his theory of stratification, Weber introduced three independent factors that form a hierarchy. These factors help explain the nature of social stratification and the complexities it brings to society. By analyzing these elements, Weber provided a more nuanced perspective on social class divisions and their implications on social structure.

Feminist legal theory includes a range of approaches aimed at analyzing and tackling gender inequality in the legal system. One such perspective is the dominance model, which views gender inequality as a result of an imbalance of power between women and men. Dominance theorists argue that the law often contributes to the subordination of women, aligning with certain aspects of critical legal theory that consider the law's potential to act as an instrument of domination. The dominance model differs from both the liberal equality model and difference theory, since its primary aim is not just to achieve equality between women and men but to free women from the restrictions of male dominance. This model recognizes that gender inequality is deeply embedded in societal structures and that legal systems frequently uphold these inequalities. Catharine MacKinnon, a leading proponent of dominance theory, contends that sexuality plays a central role in the subordination of women. She argues that women's sexuality is socially constructed by male dominance, and the sexual domination of women by men is a primary source of their general social subordination. MacKinnon argues that the legal system sustains these inequalities by enacting laws shaped by a male viewpoint. The dominance model also highlights the disparities in legal representation and access to legal aid among different groups. For instance, transgender individuals often face significant barriers in accessing legal assistance, and minority groups may experience inadequate legal representation compared to white females. In contrast, the anti-essentialist model of feminist legal theory, which emerged from the experiences of women of color and lesbians, challenges the notion of a universal female identity. This model highlights the significance of acknowledging and responding to the varied experiences and requirements of women from different racial, cultural, and sexual orientation backgrounds. By doing this, anti-essentialist feminist legal theory aims to foster a more inclusive and comprehensive view of gender inequality and how it appears in the legal system.

Decentralized exchanges (DEXs) have seen substantial growth, with more than $500 billion in trading volume during the first half of 2021. DEXs like Uniswap, Balancer, and Curve are innovative in two major ways: they enable fully decentralized trading without requiring users to hand over token custody to a third party, and they rely on automated market makers (AMMs) rather than traditional central limit order books. In AMMs, trades are executed directly with a smart contract holding liquidity reserves, with traders paying a small fee distributed among liquidity providers (LPs). Uniswap v3 introduced a new feature called concentrated liquidity, allowing LPs to supply liquidity within particular price ranges, similar to conventional market making approaches. This study examines how concentrated liquidity affects the DEX market by comparing the returns of active liquidity providers, who focus their liquidity in specific price ranges, with those of passive liquidity providers, who spread their liquidity across the full price range. Our findings indicate that concentrated liquidity has notably reduced passive LP earnings. For example, in the ETH-USDC pair, active liquidity providers now earn more in fees on average than passive liquidity providers earned before concentrated liquidity was introduced. However, this is not the case for the stablecoin pair USDT-USDC. We also examine how fundamental active strategies perform by analyzing historical trade data, calculating possible returns, and assessing their effectiveness in different market situations. For volatile pairs such as ETH-USDC, active strategies may outperform passive liquidity, yet choosing the best strategy is difficult since some fail to deliver. In contrast, for the stablecoin pair USDT-USDC, concentrated liquidity clearly surpasses passive liquidity, with a straightforward strategy selection process. Our research enhances the understanding of concentrated liquidity in DEXs through a detailed analysis of its effect on LP returns and by assessing the effectiveness of active strategies across various market conditions. This study is important because concentrated liquidity is becoming the standard AMM model, and Uniswap v3 has rapidly become the largest DEX by trading volume since its launch. Our analysis shows that the inefficiency of passive liquidity in a constant product market maker can be greatly reduced by using concentrated liquidity strategies, especially for stablecoin pairs. However, for more volatile assets, selecting the right strategy is crucial, as certain active strategies might perform worse than passive liquidity.

The KonTraG (Konzentrierte Transparenz- und Publizitätsregelungen für den Aktien- und Kapitalmarktrecht) is a German law aimed at enhancing transparency and disclosure requirements for listed companies. It highlights the significance of ongoing risk analysis and risk consolidation, along with the establishment of robust risk management systems. Under KonTraG, auditors are required to examine compliance with these new requirements, especially regarding the presence and functioning of a risk management system and the associated internal audit procedures. The audit report must include the results of this review, with the IDW test standard 340 (IDW PS 340) forming the basis for assessment. The law also stipulates that the supervisory board is responsible for appointing auditors, receiving audit reports, and involving them in the board's balance sheet meetings. All members of the supervisory board or the audit committee are required to have access to the audit reports. KonTraG applies to more than just public limited companies, including limited partnerships on shares (KGaA) and numerous limited liability companies (GmbH), particularly those with a codetermined or optional supervisory board. However, small AGs are mostly not required to comply with KonTraG regulations. Banks closely examine and assess the setup and functioning of a company-wide risk management system, like Management Risk Controlling (MRC), in line with Basel II guidelines. This is particularly relevant for companies that operate on a project basis, such as construction companies, large architectural firms, and IT system houses, where risk management is an integral part of project management tasks. Additionally, KonTraG introduces the topic of granting subscription rights to employees and members of the management board for the first time, thereby further improving corporate governance and transparency in the German market.

The legal profession has frequently been characterized as a "cartel of service providers related to society's laws," primarily aimed at limiting entry. This practice, known as 'rent-seeking' in modern economic terms, has been employed throughout history by skilled crafts and professions to increase their members' incomes by using state power to limit new entrants. For a period, Arizona did not have formal regulations for the legal profession. However, the Arizona Supreme Court recognized an inherent authority to regulate the practice of law. In 1985, Arizona's law against unauthorized legal practice was allowed to expire because of a sunset provision. Some have argued that efforts to reinstate the criminalization of unauthorized legal practice have been unsuccessful because of lingering anti-lawyer attitudes in Arizona politics. Resentment also continues from an unpopular reading of the old statute in the case of State Bar v. Arizona Land Title & Trust Co., 90 Ariz. Arizona Land Title & Trust Co., 90 Ariz. In 1961, Arizona Land Title & Trust Co., 90 Ariz. 76, imposed sanctions on a title and realty company for drafting contracts. Various jurisdictions throughout the country have established different tests to determine what constitutes the practice of law. However, none are as broad or all-encompassing as the test articulated in Arizona Title. In the U.S., professional conduct rules typically prevent lawyers from helping non-lawyers engage in the unauthorized practice of law. As a result, attorneys are not allowed to form partnerships with or share fees with non-attorneys. This regulation ensures that legal services are provided by qualified professionals, maintaining the integrity and quality of the legal profession.

Climate change, caused by the emission of greenhouse gases, is a major global issue. The Arctic region, in particular, may be experiencing a substantial release of methane and other greenhouse gases from thawing soils, which could potentially counteract political efforts to mitigate climate change. If key temperature limits are exceeded, Earth's climate might shift from an 'icehouse' to a 'greenhouse' state for the first time in 34 million years. Managing the climate crisis frequently requires shifting toward renewable energy sources. However, it's important to acknowledge that this approach also carries environmental consequences. Advocates of degrowth, steady-state economy, and circular economy theories argue that technological methods alone are insufficient for achieving sustainability. Limiting consumption is also necessary to reduce the environmental footprint. In 2019, a report named "Plastic and Climate" pointed out the major role plastic plays in contributing to greenhouse gas emissions. The report stated that plastic emitted 850 million tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) equivalents into the atmosphere in 2019. If present trends persist, emissions are expected to rise to 1.34 billion tons each year by 2030. By 2050, plastic could account for 56 billion tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to 14 percent of Earth's remaining carbon budget. This impact is in addition to the harm caused to phytoplankton. The report suggests that the only viable solution to this issue is reducing consumption. Other proposed solutions, such as biodegradable plastic, ocean cleanup, and using renewable energy in the plastic industry, may have limited effectiveness. In some cases, they could even exacerbate the problem. Another report examines the environmental and health impacts of plastic, highlighting the importance of a comprehensive strategy to tackle the issues caused by plastic pollution and its role in climate change. It is crucial to consider both the direct and indirect impacts of plastic on the environment and human health when developing strategies to mitigate these effects.

The Elementary Education Act of 1870 originally limited the availability of secondary education because of the Cockerton Judgment in 1899. At that time, the minimum school-leaving age was set at 10 years. This ruling resulted in the creation of the Education Act of 1902, commonly referred to as the Balfour Act. This act made compulsory education extend until the age of 12. At the same time, new local education authorities (LEAs) formed from the existing school boards and started to create higher-grade elementary schools or county schools, meant to work alongside the endowed grammar schools. These LEAs were allowed to build second-grade secondary schools, which eventually developed into secondary modern schools. In 1904, the Board of Education introduced regulations for secondary schools, specifying that these institutions should provide a four-year curriculum based on subjects. This curriculum was designed to culminate in a certificate covering various subjects, including English language and literature, geography, history, a foreign language, mathematics, science, drawing, manual work, physical training, and, specifically for girls, housewifery. Additional educational reforms were implemented through the Education Act of 1918, commonly referred to as the Fisher Act. This law expanded mandatory full-time education to age 14 and suggested mandatory part-time education for students aged 14 to 18. The Hadlow Report, titled "Education the Adolescent" and published in 1926, proposed a major change in the educational system by introducing a break at the age of eleven, resulting in the creation of separate primary and secondary schools. The United Nations, founded in 1945, has been committed to advancing education for everyone. However, determining the extent and nature of this commitment has proven to be a challenging endeavor. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, affirmed that access to elementary and fundamental education is a basic human right, although the exact meaning and implications of this right have been subject to interpretation and debate.

Syndicated procurement is a strategic purchasing method in which a syndicate manager combines several orders from different buyers to lower the total cost or improve delivery efficiency. This approach is also referred to as "aggregation" or "collective buying." For example, imagine a situation where five separate government agencies each need 2,000 new ergonomic office chairs. The chair manufacturer agrees to sell the chairs at $100 each for an order of 2,000 units. If each agency buys on their own, they would pay $100 per chair. However, if the manufacturer gets an order for 10,000 chairs, they are willing to lower the price to $70 per unit. By working together through a syndicate manager, the agencies can reduce the price by 30% without changing their individual orders. This approach to purchasing is common across many different industries. In the automotive industry, competing German car makers frequently place combined orders for steel to reduce costs. In a similar manner, New Zealand's Ministry of Social Development looked into using syndicated procurement to buy computers together with other government agencies in early 2010. In the United Kingdom, the Crown Commercial Service (CCS) regularly creates aggregation opportunities, allowing multiple public bodies to gain savings by leveraging their combined purchasing power. These opportunities usually function as national further competitions (NFCs) under an existing government framework agreement, which all participating organizations are required to follow. Syndicated procurement provides several advantages, such as cost reductions, simplified procurement procedures, and enhanced negotiating strength for purchasers. By combining the purchasing power of multiple buyers, organizations are able to secure more favorable terms from suppliers, resulting in lower costs and greater efficiency in procurement.

Prohibitionism is a legal and political philosophy that argues citizens will avoid certain behaviors if those actions are made illegal and strictly enforced by law enforcement. This idea has historically formed the basis for many laws, especially when a large part of the population disapproves of or is alarmed by an activity carried out by a smaller group, resulting in the legal banning of those actions. Throughout history, prohibitions have been enacted on various activities and items, including types of clothing, gambling, exotic dancing, drug use (such as alcohol and cannabis prohibitions), tobacco smoking, and firearms. Notably, the U.S. Prohibition era from 1920 to 1933, established by the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act, is widely known as "Prohibition." Likewise, the later "War on Drugs" initiative is also well recognized. Critics of prohibitionism claim that the effectiveness of these measures typically depends significantly on the successful implementation of the relevant laws. They contend that many prohibitions target victimless crimes, where the harm caused by the act is either non-existent, questionable, or confined solely to the individual committing the act. This debate underscores the continued debate about the advantages and disadvantages of prohibitionism as a legal and political approach.

The idea of autodidacticism, or self-directed learning, has long captured the attention of educators and philosophers. This educational approach highlights the significance of learners taking charge of their own learning process, employing different methods and tools to enhance their comprehension. Scaffolding techniques, as outlined by Lev Vygotsky in his 1978 publication, are crucial in assisting learners as they develop self-directed education. These methods offer temporary support to learners, helping them slowly build their problem-solving abilities and gain greater independence. One of the most outspoken critics of traditional institutionalized education was philosopher Ivan Illich. In his book *Deschooling Society*, Illich claimed that the existing school system is inherently broken. He advocated for the creation of ad-hoc co-operative networks, where autodidacts could connect with others interested in learning a specific skill or topic. These networks would allow individuals to pool their resources, materials, and knowledge, supporting one another in their learning endeavors. The rise of the internet and the World Wide Web has transformed how people approach learning. With the widespread availability of internet access, platforms such as Google, Wikipedia, YouTube, Udemy, Udacity, and Khan Academy have emerged as valuable learning centers. These resources allow people to learn together in an active and free manner, creating a collaborative setting that encourages self-directed education. Organizations like The Alliance for Self-Directed Education (ASDE) have been established to promote and provide guidance for self-directed learning. They aim to raise awareness about the benefits of this approach and offer support to those interested in pursuing self-directed education. The origins of autodidacticism can be found in the philosophical novel "Hayy ibn Yaqdhan," which made the first philosophical argument in favor of an autodidactic approach to studying nature and God. This work established the groundwork for new educational systems and the rise of new autodidacts in secular and modern societies. In conclusion, autodidacticism is a powerful approach to learning that empowers individuals to take control of their education. Thanks to scaffolding techniques, online resources, and the guidance of organizations like the ASDE, self-directed learning has grown in popularity and effectiveness as a means for people to gain knowledge and skills.

Ragging, which is a type of hazing and bullying, has remained a serious problem in Sri Lankan schools and universities, resulting in numerous tragic events. This article outlines some of the most notable cases that have occurred over the years. In 2002, a student at Hardy Technical Institute in Ampara developed kidney failure, which eventually resulted in his death. This occurred because he was made to engage in demanding physical activities and drank large quantities of alcohol. The same year, Samantha Vithanage, a third-year management student at the University of Sri Jayewardenepura, was tragically killed. Samantha Vithanage was an advocate against ragging and had started an anti-ragging campaign. During a meeting to address the issue, he found himself surrounded by a crowd of about 200 people. He was struck by shards of glass and a computer monitor was dropped on his head, which led to his death two days later. In response to the persistent issue of ragging, Prof. Chandima Wijebandara, the vice-chancellor of the University of Sri Jayewardenepura, resigned in 2006. His resignation followed when students did not follow his orders to eliminate ragging from the university. In 2014, a student named D. In 2014, a student named D. K. Nishantha was discovered hanging from a tree on the grounds of the University of Peradeniya. According to police reports, Nishantha had been a witness to the sexual assault of his friend in 2010, which was carried out by other students living in the dormitory. Following the alleged sexual assault case, Nishantha reportedly did not attend the university anymore. His death was later determined to be a suicide. In 2015, Amali Chathurika, a 23-year-old student at Sabaragamuwa University, died by suicide as a result of ragging. Similarly, in 2019, Dilhan Wijesinghe, a 23-year-old student at the University of Moratuwa, also committed suicide, with ragging being cited as the cause. These incidents highlight the severity of the ragging problem in Sri Lankan educational institutions and the need for effective measures to prevent such occurrences. Universities and colleges must enforce strict anti-ragging policies to ensure a safe and supportive environment for all students.

A writ of attachment is a legal process in which a court orders the seizure of an asset. This court order is usually given to a law enforcement officer or sheriff. The primary purpose of issuing a writ of attachment is to ensure that a judgment made by the court can be satisfied. In some legal cases, a prejudgment writ of attachment might be issued. This can occur when a plaintiff has presented strong allegations, demonstrated evidence of fraud, or if there is a risk that the defendant may attempt to dispose of or conceal assets. In these situations, the prejudgment writ of attachment functions similarly to a temporary restraining order (TRO), maintaining the status quo until the dispute is finally settled. However, unlike a TRO, a prejudgment writ of attachment can also offer the plaintiff a possible means of financial recovery. To obtain a prejudgment writ of attachment, the plaintiff is usually required to post a surety bond. The bond amount can be as high as twice the damages claimed by the plaintiff. Common reasons for seeking a prejudgment writ of attachment include allegations of fraud by the defendant or the defendant's intent to hide assets from the court. A particular kind of writ of attachment is called a "writ of body attachment," which allows a court to summon someone held in contempt before the court. In these instances, the writ may also be referred to as a "writ of bodily attachment," an "order of commitment for civil contempt," or a "warrant for civil arrest." It is important to note that the process and requirements for a writ of attachment can vary depending on jurisdiction and specific legal circumstances. For a full understanding, it is recommended to refer to appropriate legal materials or obtain guidance from a qualified legal professional.

Making thoughtful purchases and investing in pieces that represent quiet luxury are seen as smart decisions, since these items are typically crafted to have enduring appeal. Quiet luxury items, by nature, are defined by their subtle sophistication and lasting durability, making them worthwhile additions to any wardrobe or collection. These items are typically crafted with exceptional materials and attention to detail, reflecting a commitment to quality and craftsmanship. Therefore, they are able to endure the passage of time and remain valued for their beauty and functionality. Purchasing quiet luxury items can be a wise choice for multiple reasons. Firstly, they often retain their value well over time, making them a good investment for those looking to preserve or grow their wealth. Secondly, they offer versatility and can fit seamlessly into different styles and environments, keeping them consistently relevant and valued. Moreover, thoughtful buying of these items can also help foster a more sustainable and responsible way of consuming. By opting for high-quality, durable items, consumers can minimize waste and encourage a more thoughtful approach to spending. In conclusion, quiet luxury items, with their timeless appeal and exceptional craftsmanship, can be an excellent choice for those seeking to make conscientious purchasing and investment decisions. By choosing these items, people can experience the advantages of lasting quality, adaptability, and a more sustainable way of living.

The APEX Business-IT Global Case Challenge is an annual competition held in Singapore that highlights the integration of business and information technology (IT). Organized by the School of Information Systems (SIS) at Singapore Management University (SMU), this event attracts participants from over 20 universities worldwide, typically third or fourth-year students. The competition occurs every year in May and lasts between four to five days. Every year, a distinct "live" case is showcased, highlighting actual difficulties encountered by companies in the real world. Teams have 24 hours to create and present detailed solutions that use IT to tackle these challenges and meet business needs. In addition to the main competition, participants also engage in a workshop led by industry experts on a relevant topic. The event also includes social activities and business networking sessions, providing opportunities for participants to connect with professionals in the field. The APEX Business-IT Global Case Challenge has consistently received strong support from external partners, including sponsorships and company representatives serving on judging and workshop panels. Previous editions have featured notable partners such as Microsoft, IBM, Citibank, Credit Suisse, Barclays, and Deloitte. The 2016 APEX Business-IT Global Case Challenge took place from May 3 to June 6, 2016.
