They also explore the consequences of these properties for classifying unitary representations, showing that all such representations must be of the highest- or lowest-weight type under specific conditions. A major contribution of the paper is the introduction of a new graphical method for examining the algebraic structure, employing a two-dimensional lattice to depict the weight lattice and the grading functions. This method makes it simpler to understand the algebra and its representations, facilitating the identification of the conditions for the existence of unitary representations. The authors also present a proof that the $\mathfrak{su}(\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}|\mathsf{r},\mathsf{s})$ real form, with all parameters non-zero, only allows for the trivial unitary representation. This result is significant as it sets a clear boundary on the types of unitary representations that can be associated with this algebra. In addition, the paper examines how duality transformations affect the classification of unitary representations. The authors show that while some transformations can lead to a loss of the highest-weight property, others, specifically those involving $p$-odd nodes, preserve this property. This realization is essential for grasping the structure of the algebra and its representations. The paper's findings are presented in a clear and concise manner, with the authors employing a combination of mathematical proofs and graphical illustrations to convey their arguments. The researchers' use of a weight lattice to depict the fundamental weights of the algebra is an especially creative element of the study, providing a fresh approach to the classification of unitary representations. In conclusion, the paper contributes significantly to the understanding of unitary representations for the $\mathfrak{su}(\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}|\mathsf{m})$ Lie superalgebra. The authors' creative method for studying the algebraic structure and their thorough analysis of the conditions for the existence of unitary representations offer important insights for researchers in the field. The clear presentation of results along with the use of graphical methods to illustrate key concepts makes the paper accessible to a broad audience, thereby increasing its impact and relevance.

The Ljungström air preheater is a type of air preheater designed by the Swedish engineer Fredrik Ljungström (1875-1964). Ljungström obtained the patent for this invention in 1930. This innovative technology is widely used in modern utility boilers, contributing up to 20 percent of the total heat transfer in the boiler process, while representing only about two percent of the investment. In the 1920s, Ljungström's factory, workshop, and laboratory activities, along with his research facilities, were located in Lidingö and employed around 70 personnel. During the 1930s, the site was repurposed as a film studio. In the 1970s, the facilities were eventually demolished to accommodate new industrial buildings. The Ljungström air preheater has made a major difference in improving the efficiency of power plants around the world. It is estimated that this technology has saved approximately 4,960,000,000 tons of oil, making it one of the most successful fuel-saving inventions in history. The American Society of Mechanical Engineers recognized the Ljungström air preheater as the 44th International Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark in 1995. Today, the Ljungström air preheater continues to be an integral component in numerous modern power stations across the globe, enhancing their operational efficiency and reducing fuel consumption. The technology's enduring legacy is a testament to the ingenuity of its inventor, Fredrik Ljungström, and his contribution to the field of mechanical engineering.

In this section, we explore the construction of the quantum trace map, a key element of our research, and its significance for understanding ideal triangulations of punctured surfaces. We start by introducing the coordinate change map, which moves between different ideal triangulations while maintaining the consistency of the corresponding quantum traces. This map plays a key role in understanding how the quantum trace remains unchanged when the triangulation is modified. Our approach is based on the work of Bonahon and Wong, who developed the idea of a split ideal triangulation and set out the criteria for a link to be in good position with respect to this structure. This good position is crucial for defining the quantum trace on biangle components and combining it across the whole surface. We define the quantum trace for a stated skein in a biangle using the state sum method and skein relations, allowing us to extend this definition to any stated skein. This process enables us to assign a quantum trace to any framed link that is in good position relative to a split ideal triangulation. Our research introduces the quantum canonical map, a new element that assigns a specific quantum trace to every lamination on a punctured surface. The map is first defined for special laminations and then generalized to all laminations via multiplicativity. We show that this map behaves consistently across different triangulations, a characteristic essential for its use in multiple mathematical settings. Furthermore, we examine the link between the quantum trace and the Chebyshev polynomials, uncovering a relationship between matrix traces and these polynomials that plays a key role in calculating the quantum trace for laminations of higher weight. The novelty of our work stems from the thorough development of the quantum trace map and the quantum canonical map, which expand the current mathematical framework and provide novel tools for analyzing quantum surfaces and their characteristics. Our results enhance the understanding of how quantum algebraic structures interact with geometric topological features, opening new avenues for exploration in the field of quantum topology.

In the field of information technology, different design patterns help with the transfer and handling of data. These include one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many, and many-to-one relationships. Technological advances have brought about tools like blogs, wikis, Really Simple Syndication (RSS), tagging, and chat to support these patterns. An example of a one-to-one exchange model implemented by the United States government is the National Information Exchange Model (NIEM). However, it's crucial to recognize that standalone one-to-one models might not adequately meet the demands of data exploitation technologies. Advanced information sharing platforms are designed to address these needs by providing controlled vocabularies, data harmonization, and data stewardship policies and guidelines. These platforms also follow established standards to ensure consistency in data related to privacy, security, and data quality. The term "information sharing" gained prominence following the 9/11 Commission Hearings and the subsequent report on the United States government's response to information about the planned terrorist attack on the New York City World Trade Center. The report emphasized the importance of better information sharing between government agencies. In response, President Bush issued several executive orders mandating agencies to implement policies for sharing information across organizational boundaries. The 2004 Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act placed additional emphasis on the significance of information sharing. An Information Sharing Environment Program Manager (PM-ISE) was appointed to oversee the implementation of the provisions outlined in the Act. The goal was to create a more cohesive and effective approach to information sharing, enhancing national security and intelligence capabilities. In short, the development of information sharing design patterns and technologies has been shaped by the demand for better communication and collaboration across different organizations. The U.S. government has made major efforts to tackle these issues by putting in place policies and initiatives designed to improve information sharing and data exploitation abilities.

Water conditioners are specially made products intended to be added to tap water prior to using it in an aquarium. They help enhance water quality, creating a safer and more suitable environment for aquatic life. When tap water contains chlorine, a water conditioner with a dechlorinator is usually added. These products often contain sodium thiosulfate, which helps to reduce chlorine to chloride, a compound that is less harmful to fish. However, it is important to note that chloramine is now frequently used in water disinfection processes. Simple dechlorinators don't work well on chloramine and might actually release free ammonia, which can be extremely harmful to fish. To solve this problem, more advanced water conditioners have been created. These products include sulfonates, which can neutralize both chlorine and ammonia. This ensures a safer environment for fish and other aquatic organisms. The most advanced water conditioners go a step further by including chelators, such as ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA). These chelators attach to and eliminate heavy metals from the water, significantly improving the aquarium's water quality. Additionally, some water conditioners contain slime coat protectors, such as polyvinylpyrrolidones or aloe vera extracts. These substances help to protect the natural slime coat on fish, reducing stress behavior and promoting overall well-being. In short, water conditioners are essential for keeping the aquarium environment healthy and safe for aquatic life. They tackle multiple water quality problems such as chlorine, chloramine, ammonia, and heavy metals, and also help reduce stress on fish.

In molecular mechanics, the potential energy function is a key concept that describes a system's energy in terms of its atomic positions. One method of representing potential energy involves a quadratic expression based on generalized displacement forces, which correspond to the negative gradient of the potential energy. This method is especially helpful for describing chemical bonds and studying the stability of molecular structures. The potential energy, denoted as V, can be expressed as a quadratic form involving the generalized displacement forces (Gq) and a matrix C, which is the compliance matrix. The relationship is given by the following equation: \[ V = \frac{1}{2} G_q^T C G_q \quad \text{(eq. Gq is defined as the product of Hq and Q. It can be written as: \[ G_q = H_q Q \quad \text{(eq.} In this equation, Hq is a matrix that connects the displacement forces to the displacement coordinates, and Q is a vector representing the displacement coordinates. By substituting the expression for $ G_q $ from equation 6 into equation 5, we arrive at an alternative expression for the potential energy: \[ V = \frac{1}{2} Q^T H_q^T C H_q Q \quad \text{(eq. 7)} \] 7)} \] This formulation is advantageous because it is independent of the choice of coordinate system and avoids issues with redundant Hessian matrices, which can complicate the calculation of force constants in traditional methods. The compliance matrix C needs to be positive definite to ensure the potential energy is well-defined. This means that C is the inverse of the matrix Hq: \[ C = H_q^{-1} \quad \text{(eq. 8)} \] 8)} \] This relationship ensures that the potential energy is minimized when the system is in its equilibrium state, which corresponds to the lowest energy configuration. The calculation of compliance constants can be applied regardless of the redundancy of the coordinates, making it a versatile tool for analyzing molecular structures. For example, the force constants of a molecule such as cyclobutane can be determined with this method, offering valuable information about its stability and bonding features. In short, the quadratic form representation of potential energy using generalized displacement forces and the compliance matrix provides a strong framework for understanding the energetics of molecular systems. This approach is particularly useful for defining chemical bonds and analyzing the stability of molecular structures, as it is coordinate-independent and avoids complications associated with redundant Hessian matrices.

The Extended Hubbard Model (EHM) has been instrumental in elucidating phenomena such as metal-insulator transitions, antiferromagnetism, and high-temperature superconductivity. Despite its simplicity, the EHM encapsulates the fundamental characteristics of strongly correlated electron systems. However, numerous aspects of the model are still not fully understood. In our previous work, we applied the Self-Consistent Random Phase Approximation (SCRPA) to the one-dimensional EHM, demonstrating its effectiveness in treating electron correlations rigorously. Our findings revealed that repulsive off-site interactions enhance conductivity, as evidenced by the vanishing SCRPA energy gap under strong on-site and intermediate off-site repulsions. However, the one-dimensional character of the model prevents the emergence of ferromagnetism, restricting its relevance to conventional conductors. Inspired by the discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprate layers, the two-dimensional EHM has attracted considerable interest. However, solving the model in a general setting remains challenging. While an exact solution has not been achieved, various approximations have been proposed. Recently, E. Kovacs et al. Recently, E. Kovacs et al. provided an exact solution for a small 4x4 cluster of the conventional Hubbard Model, emphasizing the dynamics of electrons governed by hopping energy and on-site repulsion. In this paper, we build upon this method by applying it to the EHM, including off-site interactions characterized by the interaction energy V. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the model and outlines the computational process for building an 85x85 Hamiltonian matrix. Section 3 presents our results for ground and gap energies, discussing the impact of off-site interactions on system dynamics. Finally, Section 4 wraps up the paper. The two-dimensional EHM on a square lattice is defined by the Hamiltonian: \[ H = -\sum_{\langle i,j \rangle, \sigma} t_{ij} c_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger} c_{j,\sigma} + U\sum_{i} n_{i,\uparrow} n_{i,\downarrow} + V\sum_{\langle i,j \rangle, \sigma, \sigma'} n_{i,\sigma} n_{j,\sigma'} \] This Hamiltonian captures the hopping term \( t \), local repulsion \( U \), and nearest-neighbor repulsion \( V \). For a finite system, the model yields exact solutions for ground state energy, energy gap, and occupation numbers. We consider a 4x4 square lattice at one-eighth filling with periodic boundary conditions, leading to three possible particle configurations and corresponding states. By introducing a linear operator $ T $ and utilizing the symmetry properties of the 4x4 cluster, we reduce the 28800 possible electron distributions to 85 orthogonal cluster states. The Hamiltonian, when applied to the basis vector, results in a non-diagonal r-space basis, necessitating the definition of an 85x85 energy matrix \( E_{nm} \). Calculating eigenvalues and eigenvectors numerically enables the analysis of local properties within the lattice. Our results, shown in Figures 2 and 3, show that the ground state energy varies smoothly with the on-site interaction $ U $ and linearly with the off-site interaction $ V $. This behavior underscores the role of off-site interactions in shaping the electronic dynamics of the system.

Ophthalmology services have played a major role in Cuba's international medical efforts, especially through the Operación Milagro program. This initiative has concentrated on offering eye surgeries to Cuban, Venezuelan, and Latin American patients, both inside Cuba and in other countries. By August 2007, Cuba had conducted more than 750,000 eye surgeries at no cost, with 113,000 of those benefiting its own citizens. Since then, the program has expanded to include 69 Operación Milagro clinics in 15 countries by 2017. By 2019, the program had offered free surgeries to more than 4 million individuals in 34 countries. However, there have been claims about the program's practices. In 2017, The Miami Herald reported that defectors from the program said they felt pressured to fake documents and throw away medication because of daily patient quotas. This was reportedly due to regular audits of their supplies requiring them to match the patient count. Those who didn't meet their quotas were threatened with pay cuts or being sent back to Cuba. In addition to the Operación Milagro program, Cuba has participated in various other medical aid efforts. Since 1990, the country has provided long-term care for 24,000 victims of the Chernobyl disaster, offering treatment for hair loss, skin disorders, cancer, leukemia, and other illnesses attributed to radioactivity, all free of charge. Cuba has also sent its medical teams to countries such as Bolivia and South Africa. Following the 2005 election of Evo Morales, Cuban medical aid gained greater visibility in Bolivia. In South Africa, a 1995 cooperation agreement has enabled hundreds of Cuban doctors to work in the country. At the same time, South Africa has been sending medical professionals to Cuba, creating a mutually beneficial exchange of medical knowledge and services.

In this section, we investigate the effectiveness of our proposed method using different examples, highlighting its innovative features and contributions. We examine various subpopulations within the entire population, assigning predicted outcomes to maintain a continuous range that covers the expected outcomes of the subpopulation being analyzed. Using reliability diagrams, we differentiate between the full population (gray points and lines) and the particular subpopulation (black points and lines). Our first example looks at a mix of subpopulations that have a wide variety of expected outcomes, except for a small gap near certain scores. We choose a subpopulation with the highest expected outcomes for each score, employing a scoring system that clusters scores close to zero. The second example looks at a subpopulation where expected outcomes vary smoothly between the lowest and highest values across all subpopulations. The third example looks at a subpopulation where expected outcomes show distinct oscillations, employing a scoring system that isn't tightly clustered around zero. In the fourth example, we incorporate weighted sampling by treating the entire population as a combination of subpopulations that have fluctuating success probabilities. We choose a subpopulation with uniform success probability and add three outliers to examine their effect on the analysis. Interestingly, we find that heavily weighted observations can produce misleading results in reliability diagrams, similar to Simpson's Paradox. However, our method of comparing subpopulations via cumulative differences effectively mitigates this issue by subtracting baseline rates, similar to de-trending. Our results demonstrate that while the reliability diagrams and scalar summary statistics capture some aspects of the subpopulation's deviations, they struggle to detect high-frequency oscillations and the impact of heavily weighted observations. In contrast, our cumulative deviation plots offer a more accurate depiction of the subpopulation's expected outcomes, even though they may show some random fluctuations. Additionally, we examine the standard training dataset "ImageNet-1000," treating each of the thousand labeled classes as a distinct natural subpopulation. This analysis also supports the reliability and practical use of our method in real-world situations. Our innovative approach provides a more detailed understanding of subpopulation deviations, offering useful insights for both researchers and practitioners.

We are now adjusting our routines for the parallel PLUTO code to improve computational efficiency. Our research presents several novel features, such as taking into account radiation from the central accretion disk and stars, which affects both the heating of dust and gas and the dynamics of AGN dust tori. Our detailed radiative transfer calculations show that infrared radiation pressure plays a significant role only in the inner regions near the midplane, consistent with the results from Krolik (2007). However, radiation pressure has a negligible effect on large-scale filaments overall, except in areas that are directly illuminated, where it could potentially drive outflows along the torus axis. Future studies will focus on conducting detailed radiative transfer calculations within hydrodynamical simulations to better understand these processes. Our study also examines the effect of weak magnetic fields, which, when combined with shear from differential rotation, can lead to magneto-rotational instability, promoting accretion toward the core. Strong magnetic fields in certain areas might also result in hydromagnetic outflows, possibly increasing the torus opening angle. However, self-gravity and star formation are not yet included in our models, even though we recognize that some parts of the inner turbulent disk and filamentary structures are Jeans unstable and could potentially form stars, which aligns with the findings of Nayakshin (2006) and Paumard (2006). Future studies will include self-gravity to better model the accretion flow and the impact of supernova explosions. In addition to the central accretion disk, we also take into account the radiation contribution from stars in the post-starburst phase. Observations of Seyfert galaxies indicate that the stellar luminosity constitutes a small fraction of the central accretion disk's luminosity at this stage, so we currently disregard its impact on dynamics and heating. However, we acknowledge the significance of additional mass inflow from the galaxy, such as dusty mini-spirals, which can contribute to feeding the AGN. Our method for simulating the observed characteristics of dust tori uses hydrodynamic simulations with the TRAMP code, and then includes postprocessing to transform gas density into dust density. We use a fixed gas-to-dust ratio and consider variations in grain types and their sublimation temperatures. The resulting dust density distributions are then input into the 3D radiative transfer code MC3D to compute temperature distributions and simulate observable quantities such as spectral energy distributions (SEDs) or images across various wavelengths. Our standard model, illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:mc3d_hydro}, shows dust re-emission and central radiation at various inclination angles, serving as a reference for comparing with observational data. Our approach enables a detailed comparison with mid-infrared interferometric observations and offers constraints for modeling nuclear stellar clusters and the fueling of the central active region. In summary, our research offers a comprehensive method for modeling the dynamics and observed characteristics of AGN dust tori, taking into account radiation, magnetic fields, and additional mass contributions. Our results enhance the understanding of AGN structure and evolution, and could be further improved by including self-gravity and detailed radiative transfer calculations in future studies.

The creation of polio vaccines marked a major achievement in medical history. In the early stages, attempts were made to create a vaccine by using spinal cords from monkeys infected with the polio virus, which were then treated with formaldehyde. One such attempt was made by Dr. Brodie, who first tested the vaccine on himself and his assistants before administering it to three thousand children. While some children had allergic reactions, the vaccine failed to provide immunity against polio. A significant advancement in polio vaccine development happened in the late 1940s and early 1950s when a team led by John Enders at Boston Children's Hospital successfully grew the poliovirus in human tissue. This achievement laid the foundation for the creation of effective polio vaccines. Enders, together with his coworkers Thomas H. Weller and Frederick C. Robbins, received the Nobel Prize in 1954 for their pioneering research. Two types of polio vaccines are currently in use around the world to fight the disease. The first, developed by Jonas Salk, was tested in 1952 using the HeLa cell line and announced to the public on April 12, 1955. Known as the inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV), it consists of an injected dose of inactivated poliovirus. In 1954, the vaccine went through large-scale field trials, which at that time were the biggest medical experiments ever conducted. It was then implemented for use in the United States in 1955. After widespread immunization efforts led by the March of Dimes, the number of polio cases in the country fell sharply, dropping from almost 58,000 at its peak to just 5,600 by 1957. Eight years after Salk's breakthrough, Dr. Albert Sabin created an alternative polio vaccine called the oral polio vaccine (OPV). This vaccine employs live but weakened polioviruses that can be taken by mouth. The development of these vaccines has played a crucial role in the global effort to eradicate polio.

This section provides a detailed analysis of the cross-sections and kinematic distributions for $W$-pair production in proton-proton ($pp$) collisions at 14 TeV, with a focus on the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Tevatron. The study shows that one-loop corrections to the total cross-sections are substantial, especially for high transverse momenta or large invariant masses of the vector bosons. The authors suggest a scale choice to address these corrections and examine the scale dependence of the cross-sections, showing that next-to-leading order (NLO) results show less scale dependence, particularly when a jet veto is applied. The paper presents a new method to stabilize the perturbative expansion by implementing a jet veto, which reduces one-loop corrections and shows a consistent pattern under various conditions. The authors also examine the effect of extra cuts on the transverse momenta of charged leptons, discovering that these can greatly influence the scale dependence and the stability of the leading-order results. The novel features of this study involve a thorough analysis of scale dependence and the use of a jet veto to enhance the stability of the perturbative expansion, both of which are essential for understanding the behavior of $W$-pair production at the LHC and the Tevatron. The results offer important insights into the theoretical uncertainties associated with scale dependence and present a more reliable description of $W$-pair production at these colliders. In addition, the study provides kinematic distributions for the processes $pp \to W^-W^+ \to \ell^- \bar u \ell^{\prime +} u^\prime$ and $p \bar{p} \to W^-W^+ \to \ell^- \bar u \ell^{\prime +} u^\prime$, with emphasis on eight observables based on momenta. The Tevatron distributions are presented at both leading order (LO) and next-to-leading order (NLO), showing that NLO corrections are typically small, except for the missing transverse momentum distribution. The angular distributions behave more smoothly compared to the $p_T$-like distributions, which frequently show significant NLO corrections in their tails. This section offers a thorough examination of the cross-sections and kinematic distributions for $W$-pair production, highlighting the significance of considering scale dependence and the effect of additional cuts on the reliability of the perturbative expansion. The results provide valuable insights into the behavior of $W$-pair production at high-energy colliders.

Uptake assays are a valuable tool in determining key kinetic parameters such as Km, Ki, and Vmax, which are crucial for understanding the initial changes in ion content within cells. One way to measure these changes is by using the radioactive isotope 28Mg. This isotope decays by emitting high-energy beta or gamma particles, which can be detected with a scintillation counter. However, the half-life of 28Mg is only 21 hours, which greatly restricts its application in experiments. Since 1990, no facility has regularly produced 28Mg, and the cost of this isotope has risen, with the price per millicurie estimated to reach around US$30,000. This high cost and limited availability make it a less practical choice for many researchers. The chemical properties of Mg²+ ions are distinct, and identifying appropriate alternatives can be difficult. However, some cations like Co²+, Mn²+, and Ni²+ have been found to resemble Mg²+ in their behavior during certain enzyme reactions. Radioactive versions of these elements have been effectively used in studying cation transport. However, it's worth noting that determining the relationship between enzyme activities with the replacement ion versus the original can be challenging, potentially complicating the interpretation of results. Another way to examine the behavior of divalent cations is through the use of fluorescent indicators. Different chelators for these cations show varying fluorescence spectra when they are bound versus unbound. For calcium ions, chelators that have strong binding ability and minimal cross-interference with other ions are well established. However, Mg2+ chelators are less developed, and the main fluorescence dye used for Mg2+, Mag-Fura 2, actually has a stronger preference for Ca2+. This feature could restrict the use of this dye to certain cell types, since it might not reliably represent Mg2+ ion activity in every cellular setting.

The idea of vaccine overload is considered biologically unlikely for several reasons. Firstly, both vaccinated and unvaccinated children exhibit similar immune responses to infections unrelated to vaccines. Secondly, autism is not classified as an immune-mediated disease. Consequently, the notion that vaccines could trigger autism by overwhelming the immune system contradicts the current understanding of autism's pathogenesis. As a result, the hypothesis that vaccines cause autism has been largely discredited by the preponderance of scientific evidence. Regarding prenatal infections, research has established a correlation between schizophrenia and exposure to certain infections during pregnancy, such as rubella, influenza, and toxoplasmosis. For example, one study found that mothers who contracted influenza in their first trimester had a sevenfold higher risk of their child developing schizophrenia. This finding has important public health implications, as prevention strategies for infections involve vaccination, proper hygiene, and, for toxoplasmosis, the use of antibiotics. In animal studies, there have been theoretical worries about a possible connection between schizophrenia and the mother's immune reaction caused by viral antigens. A 2009 review concluded that there was inadequate evidence to endorse the routine use of the trivalent influenza vaccine during the first trimester of pregnancy. However, the vaccine is still recommended for use outside the first trimester and in specific cases, such as during pandemics or for women with particular health conditions. The CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists have developed guidelines for vaccination during pregnancy to protect the health and safety of both the mother and the unborn child. It is crucial to follow these recommendations to minimize the risk of prenatal infections and their potential consequences.

In this paper, we investigate the application of auxiliary inputs to tackle the difficulties posed by partial observability in reinforcement learning. Our main contributions are the introduction of new auxiliary inputs and a thorough experimental analysis that shows their effectiveness. Specifically, we propose using future predictions, general value functions, and predictive state representations to improve learning in partially observable environments. We also suggest combining different forms of auxiliary inputs to capture both past and future information, as well as using them to improve exploration strategies. Our experimental setup involves the Lobster Fishing environment, a partially observable Markov decision process (MDP) where an agent must collect rewards while dealing with stochastic transitions and reward regeneration. In Figure~\ref{fig:lobster_mdp}, we provide details on the observation vector, sources of stochasticity, and the structure of the MDP. Our experiments utilize the Sarsa(0) learning algorithm with linear function approximation and Adam optimizer, sweeping over various hyperparameters to identify the best performing configurations. We evaluate the performance of agents that use auxiliary inputs by comparing them to two baselines: an agent that relies solely on observations and an optimal agent with complete knowledge of the environment's dynamics. The observations-only agent acts as a benchmark to assess the effect of auxiliary inputs, whereas the optimal agent represents the best possible performance level. We present two primary forms of auxiliary inputs for the Lobster environment: exponential decaying traces and particle filtering. The decaying traces track the history of reward accumulation, whereas particle filtering offers an approximate belief state through particle weights. Both methods are integrated into the agent's state representation, allowing the agent to learn a policy that considers additional context beyond the immediate observation. Our results, shown in Figure~\ref{fig:lobster_pf_likelihood_3d}, demonstrate that agents using auxiliary inputs can reach performance closer to the optimal agent than the observations-only baseline. This demonstrates the potential of auxiliary inputs to mitigate the challenges of partial observability in RL. In conclusion, our work underscores the significance of incorporating auxiliary inputs in RL, especially in complex and partially observable settings. By incorporating extra information into the learning process, agents can create more resilient policies that handle uncertainties and enhance overall performance. Future research could focus on examining more advanced auxiliary inputs and their effects on exploration and generalization in reinforcement learning.

Inrush current is a phenomenon that happens when electrical devices, like incandescent lamps, are turned on. The initial surge of current can be as much as 14 times the steady-state current, and it may last for a few milliseconds in smaller lamps or several seconds in lamps of 500 watts or more. This can cause issues for control circuits and power supplies. Carbon-filament lamps, which are seldom used nowadays, have a negative temperature coefficient, causing them to draw more current as they heat up. However, these lamps do not experience an inrush current. To protect against inrush current, a resistor can be placed in series with the line to limit the current charging input capacitors. Although this method works well, it isn't very efficient, particularly in high-power applications, because the resistor creates a voltage drop and loses some power. Another approach to mitigate the effects of inrush current is the use of inrush current limiters. Negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) thermistors are widely used in switching power supplies, motor drives, and audio equipment to avoid damage from inrush current. A thermistor is a resistor that is sensitive to temperature, and its resistance changes in a significant and predictable way as the temperature changes. As the temperature of an NTC thermistor rises, its resistance decreases. When an inrush current limiter is used, it self-heats as the current begins to flow through it and warms up. This causes its resistance to drop, allowing a relatively small current to charge the input capacitors. Once the capacitors in the power supply are charged, the self-heated inrush current limiter offers little resistance in the circuit, resulting in a low voltage drop. This makes NTC thermistors a highly effective and efficient method for managing inrush current and protecting sensitive electronic components.

In the fields of telecommunications, computer networking, and programming, the term "timeout" or "time-out" encompasses a variety of concepts. It generally refers to a network parameter that initiates an event after a set period of time has elapsed. The timeout mechanism is designed to enhance the efficient use of limited resources and prevent indefinite waiting for certain actions or responses. A timeout is a set period during which a system waits for a particular event to take place. If the event doesn't happen within the designated time, the system will carry out a predefined action. Importantly, a timeout condition can be canceled if an appropriate timeout cancellation signal is received. Timeouts play a vital role in situations where a system must await an action or response. By setting a timeout, the system avoids indefinite waiting, which can be inefficient and wasteful of resources. Instead, the system performs a predetermined action after the timeout period ends, assuming that continued waiting is pointless and a new approach is required. Several examples illustrate the application of timeouts in different contexts: 1. In the Microsoft Windows and ReactOS command-line interfaces, the "timeout" command is used to pause the command processor for a specified number of seconds. This allows for a temporary halt in the execution of subsequent commands. 2. In Post Office Protocol (POP) connections, the server typically closes the connection if it remains idle for a certain period. This timeout mechanism prevents wasted resources on inactive connections, freeing them up for other users or tasks. Timeouts play a vital role in optimizing system performance and resource allocation. By establishing appropriate timeouts, systems can effectively manage their resources and react suitably to different scenarios, thus improving overall performance and user experience.

In this section, we explore the UAV-to-Ground (UAV-G) communication channel, which plays a crucial role in the segregated airspace system. We envision a straightforward setup involving a UAV and a Ground Control Station (GCS), with dedicated frequency bands for the UAV-GCS downlink and uplink. Given the operational range of UAVs, we differentiate between line-of-sight (LoS) and beyond-LoS (BLoS) communications, with our focus mainly on LoS links because of the expected prevalence of Small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (SUAVs) and Medium Altitude Long Endurance (MALE) UAVs, which generally have a limited range. The UAV-G communication channel is pivotal for various data links, each with its unique requirements. The Air-to-Ground (ATG) payload link, commonly utilized for video transmission, requires high throughput. For surveillance and acquisition (S&A) video links, both latency and throughput are critical, since these links need to be transmitted to the GCS or Air Traffic Control (ATC) for decision-making. Command and Control (C2) links, essential for UAV airworthiness, prioritize reliability and low latency, albeit with lower throughput demands. Considering these varied requirements, a flexible wideband communication system is considered suitable. Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is considered a strong contender because of its high spectral efficiency, adjustable data rates, and flexibility in using different spectrum amounts depending on availability and need. Our research focuses on wideband channel models for ATG links to identify the optimal OFDM waveform parameters. Small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (SUAVs) and Medium Altitude Long Endurance (MALE) UAVs typically fly at altitudes under 3,000 meters, with many commercial uses taking place in urban areas. Building on our earlier research, we performed a comprehensive literature review on ATG channels \cite{Jaber}. From the available wideband measurement campaigns, we identified the results from \cite{Newhall} as the most representative of the fading characteristics for SUAV and MALE channels during the en-route phase. However, these results have certain limitations, including the lack of Doppler spread data and the use of a 2.05 GHz frequency, which is not common in future SUAV and MALE operations. We extracted a power-delay-profile (PDP) prototype with a delay vector $\tau = [0\; 33\; 70\; 115\; 175\; 262\; 405\; 682]$ ns and a normalized power vector $P_{dB} = [0\; -8.7\; -9.6\; -11.3\; -13.4\; -15.2\; -17.0\; -20.2]$. The calculated Root Mean Square (RMS) delay spread is $\sigma_{t}=87.5$ ns. Our PDP prototype aligns closely with the 3GPP's rural area channel model, which, for default velocities of $v=\{120,180\}$ km/h and a classical Jakes Doppler Spectrum, suggests an RMS delay spread of $\sigma_{t}=100$ ns. Additionally, a maximum excess delay spread of $\tau_{\max}\approx 1.5$ $\mu$s was observed in \cite{Newhall}. Our key contribution is the thorough analysis and customization of existing channel models to meet the unique requirements of UAV-G communications, laying a strong groundwork for the design of efficient and dependable OFDM-based communication systems for UAV operations.

This section introduces a novel approach for constructing a Pickands function that can be flexibly fitted to data. Our method offers a highly-parameterized approximation that adheres to the constraints of a Pickands function while remaining computationally feasible. The paper is organized as follows: it begins with a review of previous Extreme Value Copula (EVC) modeling approaches, followed by a thorough explanation of our method, covering both theoretical and practical considerations. The following sections present a simulation study and real-data application, concluding with a discussion on the method's effectiveness and prospects for future research. In the related work section, we examine the classification of EVC modeling methods as either non-parametric or parametric. Non-parametric models provide more flexibility, especially for asymmetrical data, though they tend to have higher variance. Parametric models perform well in higher dimensions with mild asymmetry, especially when utilizing Khoudraji's asymmetric extension. We point out the shortcomings of current methods and introduce a semiparametric approach based on splines, drawing from recent developments in the field. Our method employs a geometric transformation that simplifies the modeling of a Pickands function by converting it into a 2-monotone function. This transformation is achieved through an affine transformation, which maps the support lines of the Pickands function onto a new coordinate system. The resulting 2-monotone function is easier to model and can be derived from the Pickands function using a one-to-one correspondence. This method enables a more adaptable and precise depiction of the Pickands function, addressing the shortcomings of current techniques. The key innovations in our research involve creating a novel semiparametric EVC model, employing splines to approximate the Pickands function, and applying the Williamson transform to model an Archimedean generator. Our work seeks to offer a more fundamentally sound and general approach to constructing the bivariate EVC family, especially regarding the handling of asymmetry.

A short circuit between the commutator and brushes in electric motors can result in various problems. When the power output reaches several hundred watts, this short can lead to serious commutator overheating, brush damage, and in the case of metallic brushes, possible welding between the brushes and the commutator. It's worth noting that carbon brushes, which are widely used, would not weld. This kind of short circuit is very inefficient because it quickly depletes batteries and requires power supply components to be designed to much higher standards than needed for the motor to function without the shorting. To address this problem, one possible solution is to create a gap between the commutator plates that is larger than the ends of the brushes. This approach not only eliminates the shorting issue but also increases the zero-torque range of angular positions. When a motor with this modification is spun by an external force, it will keep spinning. Additionally, it can be effectively disabled by stalling it in a position within the zero-torque angle range, where the commutator is not in contact with the brushes. This design is occasionally used in homemade hobby motors, like those built for science fairs, and appears in certain published science project books. However, this straightforward approach has a noticeable drawback. The motor now glides through a significant portion of its rotation twice each turn, with torque being pulsed. While this might work for applications such as electric fans or keeping a flywheel spinning, it doesn't meet the needs of many other situations. For instance, it would be unsuitable for driving the capstan of a tape transport or any similar application where continuous, uninterrupted torque is required.

The Tsunami UDP Protocol is a high-speed file transfer protocol created to function effectively on network paths that have a high bandwidth-delay product. It was specifically designed to overcome the limitations of standard TCP, which frequently faces efficiency challenges in those network environments. The Tsunami protocol was developed at the Advanced Network Management Laboratory at Indiana University. The protocol enables file transfers by splitting the file into a sequence of numbered blocks, each around 32 kilobytes in size. This approach facilitates efficient data transfer by making the best use of the available bandwidth. Communication between the client and server is handled through a low-bandwidth TCP connection, which coordinates the transfer process. In contrast, the actual data is sent via UDP, taking advantage of its capability to efficiently handle large amounts of data at high speeds. Using TCP for control communication and UDP for data transfer, the Tsunami UDP Protocol offers a flexible solution for high-speed file transfers in difficult network conditions. It is especially valuable in situations where the bandwidth-delay product is large, such as in long-distance or satellite networks. For further details and resources on the Tsunami UDP Protocol, interested readers are encouraged to visit the project's SourceForge page, where they can find additional information, documentation, and community support.

In this study, we explore the new area of Zero-Knowledge Zero-Shot Learning (ZK-ZSL), which represents a major improvement over Generalized Zero-Shot Learning (GZSL) and Open-Set Recognition (OSR). The ZK-ZSL framework is designed to recognize categories from the source dataset and distinguish new, unseen categories without prior knowledge, while also reconstructing their semantic features. This study tackles two major challenges in ZK-ZSL: accurately classifying unseen objects without existing labels, and the lack of semantic information for these new categories, which can result in biased predictions. Our approach innovatively recovers the clustering structures for both seen and unseen categories in the target dataset, using source labels to guide the centroids of the observed classes. We propose a distinctive structural alignment loss that improves the semantic understanding of unseen categories by leveraging their recovered clustering structures. Through extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets, our method shows better results in classification accuracy and semantic recovery, confirming the effectiveness of our new contributions. To further validate our approach, we performed a hyperparameter analysis on the AWA2 dataset, investigating how changing the prediction loss and structural alignment loss parameters, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, affects performance. We discovered that the best classification and semantic recovery accuracies occur when both parameters are set to 1.0, highlighting the reliability of our default parameter setup. The analysis showed an inverted U-shaped relationship between the parameters and performance metrics, suggesting a delicate balance that our method handles effectively. In conclusion, our work introduces a groundbreaking approach in the field of visual recognition, expanding the possibilities of what can be achieved in zero-shot learning scenarios. The novel elements of our research, such as the structural alignment loss and the method's ability to handle unseen categories, play a major role in advancing knowledge in this area.

Cancer spreading to the pelvic wall can cause pain in one of the iliac fossae. Patients who experience pain while walking severe enough to keep them confined to bed may have cancer that has attached to or spread into the iliacus muscle. Hypogastric pain, which is found between the navel and the pubic bone, is commonly linked to cancers of the uterus and bladder. It may also occur in colorectal cancer, especially when the tumor invades or adheres to the uterus or bladder. Visceral pain, which originates from internal organs, is generally diffuse and difficult to locate. It is commonly referred to more distant and usually superficial areas. For example, acute bleeding into a hepatocellular carcinoma can lead to severe pain in the upper right abdomen, which might be life-threatening and require emergency surgery or other immediate treatments. A tumor can cause the liver to grow substantially, stretching its capsule and resulting in aching pain in the right upper abdomen. Other causes of pain in an enlarged liver include: - Traction of the supporting ligaments when standing or walking - The liver pressing against the rib cage or pinching the abdominal wall - Straining the lumbar spine - In some postures, the liver may pinch the parietal peritoneum against the lower rib cage, resulting in sharp, transient pain that is relieved by changing position Additionally, a tumor may infiltrate the liver's capsule, causing dull or occasionally stabbing pain. In contrast, kidney and spleen cancers usually cause less pain than liver tumors. Kidney tumors typically cause pain only when the organ has been significantly affected. Keep in mind that the information given here is general and might not be applicable to every situation. Diagnosis and treatment must always be guided by a comprehensive medical assessment performed by a properly trained healthcare provider.

This section presents different approaches for approximating multivariate probability density functions, which play a key role in performing efficient Bayesian inference in high-dimensional settings. We start by estimating Gaussian distributions, using a full covariance matrix for up to four dimensions and a diagonal covariance matrix for higher dimensions, scaled by a factor obtained from the normal reference rule. For mixture models, we suggest using Gaussian mixtures with parameters estimated via expectation-maximization, and the number of components is chosen according to the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). When the prior distribution is bounded, we propose truncated Gaussian mixtures that include known bounds as part of the mixture components. We also investigate the application of vine copulas to break down multivariate distributions into marginal components and a copula function that models dependency structures. The optimal copula function is chosen by minimizing the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), and the vine structure is determined using a maximum spanning tree with Kendall's tau edge weights. In terms of marginal distributions, we consider empirical distribution functions, Pareto tails to enhance accuracy in the tails, and parametric mixtures for both unbounded and bounded variables. The parameters of these distributions are estimated via expectation-maximization, with the number of components chosen to minimize the BIC. For regression-based density estimation, we use Gaussian process regression, which is flexible and naturally accommodates multivariate regressors. The Gaussian process is normalized by computing its integral and applying a normalizing constant to ensure it integrates to one. We test two covariance functions—the squared exponential and the Matérn kernel with ν=3/2—by optimizing the length scale parameter via cross-validation. Lastly, we address the application of importance reweighting, which utilizes the original Monte Carlo samples for direct weighting, acting as a benchmark for the approximation techniques discussed. This method highlights the novel contributions of our work, offering a complete set of tools for approximating multivariate probability density functions in Bayesian inference.

Fiber optic communication has transformed telecommunications by enabling high-speed data transmission with very little signal loss. The technology first showed its potential in Long Beach, California, where fiber optics enabled a 6 Mbit/s data transfer rate. This advancement opened the door to the broad use of fiber optics in telecommunications networks. One of the first wide area network fiber optic cable systems was installed by Rediffusion in Hastings, East Sussex, UK, in 1978. The system used cables installed in ducts across the town, providing service to more than 1000 subscribers. At that time, the main function of these cables was to carry television channels that couldn't be received locally. The first transatlantic telephone cable to use optical fiber technology was TAT-8, which relied on Desurvire's optimized laser amplification technology. This innovative cable came online in 1988, significantly strengthening the role of fiber optics in worldwide telecommunications. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, industry advocates and research firms like KMI and RHK forecasted a major surge in demand for communication bandwidth. This increase was due to the rising popularity of the Internet and the expansion of bandwidth-heavy consumer services, like video on demand. The rapid growth of Internet Protocol (IP) data traffic exceeded the growth in integrated circuit complexity, as outlined by Moore's Law. Grasping the full impact of fiber optics requires understanding the fundamental components of a telecommunication system. A transmitter, which serves as the information source, converts information into a signal that can be transmitted. In electronics and telecommunications, a transmitter or radio transmitter is an electronic device that, using an antenna, produces radio waves. These radio waves are essential for broadcasting and are a vital component of many electronic devices that communicate wirelessly. The integration of fiber optics into telecommunication systems has significantly enhanced data transmission capabilities, enabling faster and more reliable communication across vast distances. As technology keeps evolving, fiber optics will play an even bigger role in telecommunications, continuing to influence how we connect and exchange information in the digital era.

Placentophagy, which involves eating the placenta, can be shaped by both spiritual beliefs and practical factors. In certain cultures, like in Saudi Arabia, traditional customs for honoring the placenta may involve burial instead of eating it. These practices often involve waiting to sever the umbilical cord until it stops pulsing, which helps prevent blood loss and infection, and maintaining the placental connection until after delivery and the onset of nursing. While placentophagy is not common in most modern human cultures, it became somewhat notable in 2012 when American actress January Jones stated that consuming her placenta aided her in returning to work sooner after childbirth. Placentophagy has been recorded in some modern societies. For instance, in the 1960s, a Czechoslovakian medical officer noted that Vietnamese nurses and midwives from Chinese and Thai backgrounds ate the placentas of young, healthy patients for unknown reasons. The placentas were prepared by removing the membranous parts and frying them with onions before consumption. A cross-cultural ethnographic study carried out by researchers from the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, examined 179 modern human societies and found examples of placentophagy. This study underscores the diverse cultural approaches to birthing practices and the various ways in which the placenta is handled and revered in different societies. It's worth noting that although some people may opt to eat the placenta for personal or cultural reasons, the scientific evidence backing its health benefits is still limited and not fully established.

In this paper, we examine the perturbative definition of scattering amplitudes, which are traditionally grounded in quantum field theory and defined through Feynman vertices and diagrams. We investigate an alternative framework in which amplitudes are fundamental, and the $S$-matrix is built from a minimal set of data and rules known as a "diagrammar." Our method relies on defining the $S$-matrix via its singularities, a concept that has continued to be a rich and active area of study. Our main contribution is building an $S$-matrix for a theory of Einstein gravity with $R^3$ terms, based on the singularity structure of three-point amplitudes. We work within the framework of massless theories, using twistor variables to represent amplitudes with a clearly defined "spinor weight." Our theory starts with the standard three-point amplitudes of Einstein gravity and is extended by including additional three-point amplitudes that involve higher powers of momenta. These extensions are non-trivial and can only depend on either $\spa{i}.j$ or $\spb{i}.j$. The core of our approach lies in requiring amplitudes to display the appropriate symmetries and singularities. We show that the full $S$-matrix can be reconstructed from these vertices by enforcing the amplitudes to factorize on simple poles. This factorization is made possible through two important shifts: the original Britto-Cachazo-Feng-Witten (BCFW) shift and the Risager shift. Both shifts convert the momenta into functions of a complex variable $z$, maintaining the null conditions and overall momentum conservation. We focus on the leading contribution from $\alpha$ to the $S$-matrix, analyzing both four-point and five-point amplitudes. For the four-point amplitudes, we show that the all-plus amplitudes are non-zero and display the correct symmetries when applying the suitable shift. In contrast, the single minus amplitude requires the BCFW shift. For five-point amplitudes, we obtain an all-plus amplitude that preserves complete crossing symmetry and does not depend on an arbitrary spinor. Our findings are in agreement with earlier calculations based on field theory and also match the UV divergent parts of gravity across different dimensions. This study highlights the effectiveness of on-shell recursive techniques in calculating scattering amplitudes and offers a new viewpoint on building the $S$-matrix from a minimal set of amplitudes.

Leprosy, also called Hansen's disease, is a long-term infectious illness caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae. It mainly targets the skin, peripheral nerves, respiratory system, and mucous membranes in the upper respiratory tract. Early detection and treatment using multidrug therapy (MDT) are essential to avoid complications like nerve damage and disability. In Indonesia, the prevalence rate of leprosy in the 21st century is slightly under one new case per 10,000 people, with approximately 20,000 new cases detected each year. However, the rate is significantly higher in certain regions, particularly South Sulawesi, where there are more than three new cases per 10,000 people, and North Maluku, with more than five new cases per 10,000 people. The Indonesian government provides MDT free of charge to patients who require it. Several hospitals in major population centers are specifically designed to meet the medical needs of individuals affected by the disease. Even with better early detection and treatment options, around 10% of patients in Indonesia have already suffered serious nerve or other damage before their condition is diagnosed and addressed. This is frequently caused by a lack of awareness and the widespread stigma linked to leprosy, which prevents individuals from seeking treatment. To combat this stigma and eliminate discrimination against people with leprosy, PERMATA (Perhimpunan Mandiri Kusta) Indonesia was established in 2007. The organization was founded by a group of individuals who had all been treated for leprosy. They worked to establish connections with key figures among those with the disease in communities in South Sulawesi, East Java, and NTT—three provinces with some of the highest incidence rates of leprosy in the country. Efforts to increase awareness, inform the public, and assist those impacted by leprosy are crucial for minimizing the disease's effects in Indonesia. By addressing the social and medical challenges associated with leprosy, the country can work towards a future where no one suffers from the consequences of this ancient and curable disease.

High-power radio frequency devices are essential in many applications, such as industrial radio frequency heating, particle accelerators, and broadcast transmitters. This is particularly important at microwave frequencies, where components such as klystrons and traveling-wave tubes are employed to achieve amplification at power levels that semiconductor devices cannot currently reach. The typical home microwave oven is a common example of a device that effectively generates microwave power, using a magnetron tube to produce hundreds of watts. Although solid-state devices made from materials like gallium nitride offer promising alternatives, they remain in their early developmental stages and are currently quite costly. In military applications, high-power vacuum tubes can generate signals in the range of 10 to 100 megawatts, which can potentially damage an unprotected receiver's frontend. These devices are categorized as non-nuclear electromagnetic weapons and were initially developed in the late 1990s by both the United States and Russia. In the music industry, tube amplifiers remain commercially viable in certain niche markets. They are highly prized for their warm tone, responsive overdrive, and capacity to mimic the sound of vintage tube recordings. This contributes to their widespread use in audiophile gear, guitar amplifiers, and studio equipment. Many guitarists favor valve amplifiers over solid-state ones because of their distinctive distortion characteristics when overdriven. It's worth noting that any amplifier can only faithfully amplify a signal up to a specific volume. Once this limit is exceeded, the amplifier starts to distort the signal. Different circuits will cause varying degrees and types of distortion, which can be a desirable feature for some musicians.

Organoastatine chemistry involves the study of organoastatine compounds, which are chemical compounds containing a carbon-astatine bond. Astatine, a highly radioactive element, possesses the longest-lived isotope, 210At, which has a half-life of just 8.1 hours. Because of its radioactivity, organoastatine chemistry can only be studied through tracer methods with extremely small amounts. The challenges from radiation damage, along with the difficulties in separation and identification, are greater for organic astatine compounds than for inorganic ones. Most research in organoastatine chemistry focuses on 211At, an isotope that has a half-life of 7.21 hours. This isotope is especially valuable in nuclear medicine because it is more effective at targeting and destroying abnormal thyroid tissue compared to 131I. Astatine-labeled iodine reagents have been utilized to synthesize various organoastatine compounds, including RAt, RAtCl2, R2AtCl, and RAtO2, where R represents phenyl or p-tolyl groups. Alkyl and aryl astatides are fairly stable and have been studied at elevated temperatures (up to 120 °C) through radio gas chromatography. Demercuration reactions have also been used to generate small amounts of 211At-containing aromatic amino acids, steroids, and imidazoles, as well as other compounds. Astatine exhibits both halogen-like and metallic properties, which means that analogies with iodine can sometimes be applicable, but not always. Astatine can be incorporated into organic molecules using several methods, including halogen exchange, halodediazotation (which replaces a diazonium group), halodeprotonation, or halodemetallation. Despite the challenges associated with the radioactivity of astatine, organoastatine chemistry continues to be an important area of research, with potential applications in nuclear medicine and the development of new radiopharmaceuticals.

The golden ratio, commonly represented by the Greek letter φ (phi), is a mathematical constant that has fascinated mathematicians and artists for centuries. It is defined as the ratio of two quantities where the sum of the quantities and the larger quantity are equal, expressed as φ = a/b. This ratio is approximately 1.618033988749895. The golden angle, which is closely connected to the golden ratio, is the angle formed at the center of a circle by an arc that corresponds to a portion of the circle's circumference. This fraction is equal to the reciprocal of the golden ratio, which can be written as f = b/(a+b) = 1/(1+φ). Since 1 + φ equals φ squared (φ^2), the fraction f simplifies to 1/φ^2. This implies that φ^2 golden angles can fit within a full circle. The golden angle's numerical value can be approximated by multiplying the fraction f by the full circle angle, which is either 360 degrees or 2π radians. Thus, the golden angle $ g $ can be calculated as follows: in degrees, $ g \approx 360 \times 0.381966 \approx 137.50778^\circ $; in radians, $ g \approx 2\pi \times 0.381966 \approx 2.39996 $ radians. The golden angle appears fascinatingly in nature, especially in the field of phyllotaxis, which examines how leaves are arranged on a stem. A well-known example is the arrangement of florets in a sunflower, where the angle between neighboring florets is closely related to the golden angle. This arrangement is thought to enhance the packing efficiency of the florets, ensuring an optimal spread of sunlight and resources. The importance of the golden angle in nature has been explored through mathematical models, which propose that the patterns found in sunflowers and other plants could emerge naturally from solving a nonlinear partial differential equation on a flat surface. This shows how closely mathematics is linked to the natural world, with the golden angle playing a central role in the complex patterns seen in nature.

In this section, we explore the detailed aspects of our research, which focuses on the mathematical structures of algebraic curves and their corresponding fields. We start by presenting a new method for analyzing the multiplicative structure of these fields, which we denote as $F^{\ast}$. Our methodology hinges on the concept of a 'factorized form', which allows us to express every element $f$ in $F^{\ast}$ as a product of simpler components, each associated with a pair of points on the curve. This factorization is underpinned by a set of multiplicative constants, which we carefully select to ensure consistency across the entire curve. We then introduce a proposition that formalizes our approach, showing that it is indeed possible to select these constants in a manner that meets our factorization formula for every element of $F^{\ast}$. The proof of this proposition relies on the algebraic structures of the curve and its associated fields, utilizing principles like the Weil reciprocity law. Our research also explores the concept of ideles, which are elements of a field that exhibit specific multiplicative properties. We present a family of ideles that have a distinctive property, enabling them to be written in terms of the logarithmic difference of their components. This family of ideles acts as an algebraic counterpart to the classical Schottky-Klein prime form, a multi-valued function with a long and significant history in complex analysis. In the case of genus zero curves, we give explicit formulas for our ideles and the corresponding constants, serving as a concrete illustration of our abstract ideas. We also introduce algebraic counterparts of multiplicative multi-valued functions, which play a crucial role in understanding the structure of fields linked to algebraic curves. Our work concludes with the introduction of local quantum field theories, which serve as mathematical models for describing physical phenomena at a local scale. We examine three distinct types of these theories, each associated with a different algebraic structure: the Heisenberg Lie algebra, the lattice Lie algebra, and a central extension of the multiplicative group by the tame symbol. The Heisenberg Lie algebra, a central extension of the geometric loop algebra, is a cornerstone of our local quantum field theories. We define this algebra along with its associated modules, which are essential for understanding the algebraic structure of our fields. Our definitions are based on the continuous bilinear form, which plays a fundamental role in the algebraic structure of the field. In summary, our research offers a novel perspective on the algebraic structure of fields associated with algebraic curves, introducing new concepts and methodologies that have the potential to enrich our understanding of these mathematical constructs. Our work is characterized by a blend of abstract algebraic theory and concrete examples, providing a comprehensive exploration of the topic.

Acupuncture, an ancient Chinese medical practice, has a long history based on various belief systems centered around celestial and earthly bodies. These systems held that specific elements aligned at particular times, which affected the efficacy of acupuncture treatments. As Needham and Lu describe, acupuncturists of the time employed intricate charts and precise terminology to represent these "arbitrary predictions" (Needham and Lu, 140–41). During this time, acupuncture needles were much thicker than today's, often resulting in infections. Unlike today's understanding of sterilization, it was commonly thought that infections arose from using the incorrect needle, inserting it at the wrong location, or doing so at an inappropriate time (Needham and Lu, 102–03). To address this, needles were sometimes boiled in water or held over a flame and occasionally used while still warm to produce a cauterizing effect at the injection site (Needham and Lu, 104). The Great Compendium of Acupuncture and Moxibustion, published in 1601, suggested using nine needles. This number might have been shaped by the ancient Chinese view that nine possessed magical significance (Needham and Lu, 102–03). Other belief systems suggested that the human body functioned according to a rhythm, and acupuncture should be administered at the right moment within this rhythm to achieve the best results (Needham and Lu, 140–41). Some belief systems also viewed imbalances between Yin and Yang as a possible cause of illness (Needham and Lu, 140–41). The first century AD was a key time for acupuncture's development, as the initial books on the topic were published and pioneering acupuncturists started to appear. One of these early texts was the Zhen Jiu Jia Yi Jing, which appeared in the mid-3rd century AD.

High Dynamic Range Imaging (HDRI) is a method that allows for capturing and displaying a broader spectrum of light levels compared to standard imaging systems. This technology is particularly useful in scenarios where the contrast between the brightest and darkest areas is significant, such as in outdoor photography or computer graphics. The creation of HDRI in computer graphics has been closely linked to progress in shader technology, which are small programs that control how graphics are displayed on a screen. Advancements in shader models have been essential in allowing the creation of high-dynamic-range images. The first version of Shader Model 1.0, released with DirectX 8 in the early 2000s, introduced standard lighting, which helped illuminate 3D environments. However, this method had limitations. The lighting precision was limited to 8-bit integers, restricting the contrast ratio to 256:1. This meant that the brightest white was only 255 levels brighter than the darkest shade above pure black. Furthermore, lighting calculations used integers, which couldn't precisely reflect the real-world variation of light intensities, which can change continuously. On December 24, 2002, Microsoft launched DirectX 9.0, featuring Shader Model 2.0. This update was a significant step towards enabling the rendering of high-dynamic-range images. Shader Model 2.0 allowed for lighting precision beyond the 8-bit limitation, with programmers having the option to use up to 24 bits for lighting precision. While most calculations remained based on integers, the enhanced precision offered a more accurate depiction of lighting in three-dimensional environments. One of the first graphics cards to support DirectX 9.0 natively was ATI's Radeon 9700. However, it took several years for game developers to fully harness the power of Shader Model 2.0 in their games. On August 23, 2003, Microsoft released an updated version of DirectX, 9.0b, which included the Pixel Shader 2.x. This update further improved the capabilities of shader technology, laying the groundwork for more advanced rendering techniques and a more realistic depiction of high-dynamic-range images in computer graphics.

Digital twins, as virtual replicas of physical entities, are revolutionizing various sectors by offering real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and optimization. This paper explores the application of digital twins in education, smart cities, transportation, energy, and other industries, highlighting their potential to transform traditional practices. In education, digital twins can provide tailored learning experiences through the use of AI-powered assistants and adaptive learning systems. They can help close the gap between industry demands and academic programs, promoting focused talent growth. For instance, Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) can benefit from AI-powered personalization, enhancing the effectiveness of teaching and learning. In the context of smart cities, digital twins can engage citizens in city planning, optimize energy consumption, and improve transportation systems. They can also enable real-time monitoring and control of urban infrastructure, enhancing sustainability and efficiency. Smart grids, for example, can leverage digital twins for dynamic power usage management and predictive maintenance. Our research introduces an innovative approach to digital twin development, focusing on five key enabling technologies: physics-based modeling, data-driven modeling, big data cybernetics, infrastructure and platforms, and human-machine interfaces. Physics-based modeling, despite its limitations, remains a cornerstone of digital twin development, offering a foundation for understanding physical phenomena. Our approach combines experimental and numerical modeling techniques to create accurate and reliable digital twins. Data-driven modeling, on the other hand, leverages machine learning and AI algorithms to analyze large datasets, enabling predictive analytics and decision-making. This approach complements physics-based modeling, providing insights into complex systems that are difficult to model using traditional methods. Big data cybernetics is also a key part of our approach, tackling issues related to data security, management, and quality. By leveraging big data, we can create more precise and resilient digital twins capable of adapting to evolving conditions and environments. Infrastructure and platforms are essential for supporting the development and deployment of digital twins. Our research explores the use of cloud computing, IoT, and other technologies to create scalable and flexible digital twin platforms that can cater to diverse application needs. Finally, human-machine interfaces play a crucial role in ensuring the usability and accessibility of digital twins. Our approach centers on creating intuitive and interactive interfaces that enable smooth communication between users and digital twins, thereby improving user experience and supporting better decision-making. In conclusion, our research presents a comprehensive and innovative approach to digital twin development, addressing the common challenges and leveraging enabling technologies to create impactful solutions across various sectors. By combining physics-based modeling, data-driven modeling, big data cybernetics, infrastructure and platforms, and human-machine interfaces, we can unlock the full potential of digital twins and drive the digital transformation of industries.

Taste is a complex sensory experience shaped by multiple factors. The flavor of a food product depends not only on the natural aromas from the ingredients and added flavorings, but also on other components such as flavor enhancers, sweeteners, acidulants, and salt substitutes. Polyols such as sorbitol and maltitol function as carriers in flavorings and also provide a sweet taste to the product. Interestingly, the color of food can greatly influence how sweet it is perceived to be. A study discovered that increasing the red color in a drink made it taste sweeter, with darker versions being rated 2-10% higher in sweetness than lighter ones, even though they contained less sugar. Food manufacturers frequently take advantage of this effect, as illustrated by the different colors of products such as Froot Loops cereal and Gummy Bears, which often share the same flavorings. Flavor enhancers, also referred to as taste enhancers, are umami or "savory" substances that boost the taste of food without acting as flavorings themselves. They are mainly derived from amino acids and nucleotides and are commonly found as sodium or calcium salts. The European Union acknowledges and approves specific umami flavorings. In Europe, according to EU legislation, substances that only have a sweet, sour, or salty taste are not classified as flavorings (Article 2, Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008). Furthermore, under EU legislation, flavor enhancers are categorized as additives instead of flavorings (Point 14 of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008). This distinction is important for the regulation and labeling of food products in the European market.

Our experiments on synthetic data are designed to evaluate the performance of our proposed \textsc{Memorize} method in controlled settings, utilizing metrics and baselines that are not present in real-world datasets. We assess \textsc{Memorize} using two main metrics: recall probability at a later time and forgetting rate. These metrics enable us to evaluate both long-term and short-term retention by varying the value of $\tau$. We compare Memorize with three baseline methods: uniform, last-minute, and threshold-based reviewing schedules.
